# Coors Light Music Fest Concert Series at Alton Wood River Sportsmen's Club Begins July 18th Jun 26, 2014 2:45 PM 0 CommentsSave Listen to the story [Audio 1](https://s3.amazonaws.com/riverbender/mp3/storyaudio/4590.mp3) ![Image 6: facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg)Share ![Image 7: twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg)Post ![Image 8: flipboard sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/flipboard.svg)Flip ![Image 9: linkedin sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/linkedin.svg)Share ![Image 10: messenger sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/messenger.svg)Share ![Image 11: email sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/email.svg)Email ![Image 12: sharethis sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/sharethis.svg)Share (Godfrey, IL – June 25, 2014) The Coors Light Music Fest Concert Series, brought to you by Triple Jam Production, kicks off Friday, July 18th with Jake's Leg and The Brothers in a tribute to the Grateful Dead and The Allman Brothers Band. Jake's Leg was formed in 1975 and have played to thousands of people, cutting across age and lifestyle demographics. The Brothers is a St. Louis-based band that includes seven members with Todd Brennan as lead vocalist. On Friday, August 1st, get ready for the return of Think Floyd and Pepperland as they pay tribute to Pink Floyd and the Beatles. Think Floyd, which was recently voted by fans as Chicago’s favorite Pink Floyd tribute band, consists of eight members. Formed in autumn of 1996, Pepperland has played together in various incarnations and projects for over 15 years, making this sextet less a Beatles “cover” band and more a “band,” first and foremost, that plays the music of The Beatles. [Sign in to hide this notification.](https://account.riverbender.com/?redirect=true) ### Get The Latest News! Don't miss our top stories and need-to-know news everyday in your inbox. The season comes to a close on Saturday Aug. 16 with country superstars **Big & Rich** and **Jana [![Image 13](https://static.riverbender.com/media/6261424514-footerlogo.jpg)](https://static.riverbender.com/media/6261424514-footerlogo.jpg)Kramer**. The concert will also feature the supporting acts local legends Glendale Riders, Jac Freeze, Broseph E. Lee and The Harmans. Big & Rich will be supporting their newly released album and have been nominated for the "2014 CMT Country Duo Of The Year." This show will feature a tribute to our US Troops in conjunction with A Hero's Welcoming. The July 18th and August 1st concerts begin at 6 p.m. and close at 11 p.m. The Alton Wood River Sportsmen's Club is located at 3109 Godfrey Rd, Godfrey, IL 62035. Tickets are $10. Article continues after sponsor message The August 16th concert begins at 12 noon and closes at 11 p.m. Tickets are $30-$50 and are available at [www.CoorsLightMusicFest.com](http://www.coorslightmusicfest.com/?utm_source=riverbender&utm_medium=article_link). Food and beverages will be available for purchase. No coolers allowed. Concertgoers are encouraged to bring lawn chairs or blankets. Sponsors for the Coors Light Music Fest Concert Series include: Coors Light, 93.7 The Bull, Ted's Motorcycle World, Atlantis Pools, Colman's Country Campers, Helitech, 1st MidAmerican Credit Union, Grafton Winery, Joe K's, RFT-Riverfront Times, Outrageous Outdoors, Oldies 103.3 KLOU, Holiday Inn, Laura Buick GMC, Freer Auto Body, Norton & Rain Inc., Data Tronics, Re/Max Lisa Funk, Alton Wood River Sportsmen's Club, and A Hero's Welcoming. # Coors Light Music Fest Concert Series at Alton Wood River Sportsmen's Club Begins July 18th Jun 26, 2014 2:45 PM 0 CommentsSave Listen to the story [Audio 1](https://s3.amazonaws.com/riverbender/mp3/storyaudio/4590.mp3) ![Image 6: facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg)Share ![Image 7: twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg)Post ![Image 8: flipboard sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/flipboard.svg)Flip ![Image 9: linkedin sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/linkedin.svg)Share ![Image 10: messenger sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/messenger.svg)Share ![Image 11: email sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/email.svg)Email ![Image 12: sharethis sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/sharethis.svg)Share (Godfrey, IL – June 25, 2014) The Coors Light Music Fest Concert Series, brought to you by Triple Jam Production, kicks off Friday, July 18th with Jake's Leg and The Brothers in a tribute to the Grateful Dead and The Allman Brothers Band. Jake's Leg was formed in 1975 and have played to thousands of people, cutting across age and lifestyle demographics. The Brothers is a St. Louis-based band that includes seven members with Todd Brennan as lead vocalist. On Friday, August 1st, get ready for the return of Think Floyd and Pepperland as they pay tribute to Pink Floyd and the Beatles. Think Floyd, which was recently voted by fans as Chicago’s favorite Pink Floyd tribute band, consists of eight members. Formed in autumn of 1996, Pepperland has played together in various incarnations and projects for over 15 years, making this sextet less a Beatles “cover” band and more a “band,” first and foremost, that plays the music of The Beatles. [Sign in to hide this notification.](https://account.riverbender.com/?redirect=true) ### Get The Latest News! Don't miss our top stories and need-to-know news everyday in your inbox. The season comes to a close on Saturday Aug. 16 with country superstars **Big & Rich** and **Jana [![Image 13](https://static.riverbender.com/media/6261424514-footerlogo.jpg)](https://static.riverbender.com/media/6261424514-footerlogo.jpg)Kramer**. The concert will also feature the supporting acts local legends Glendale Riders, Jac Freeze, Broseph E. Lee and The Harmans. Big & Rich will be supporting their newly released album and have been nominated for the "2014 CMT Country Duo Of The Year." This show will feature a tribute to our US Troops in conjunction with A Hero's Welcoming. The July 18th and August 1st concerts begin at 6 p.m. and close at 11 p.m. The Alton Wood River Sportsmen's Club is located at 3109 Godfrey Rd, Godfrey, IL 62035. Tickets are $10. Article continues after sponsor message The August 16th concert begins at 12 noon and closes at 11 p.m. Tickets are $30-$50 and are available at [www.CoorsLightMusicFest.com](http://www.coorslightmusicfest.com/?utm_source=riverbender&utm_medium=article_link). Food and beverages will be available for purchase. No coolers allowed. Concertgoers are encouraged to bring lawn chairs or blankets. Sponsors for the Coors Light Music Fest Concert Series include: Coors Light, 93.7 The Bull, Ted's Motorcycle World, Atlantis Pools, Colman's Country Campers, Helitech, 1st MidAmerican Credit Union, Grafton Winery, Joe K's, RFT-Riverfront Times, Outrageous Outdoors, Oldies 103.3 KLOU, Holiday Inn, Laura Buick GMC, Freer Auto Body, Norton & Rain Inc., Data Tronics, Re/Max Lisa Funk, Alton Wood River Sportsmen's Club, and A Hero's Welcoming. # 1923-1975: Pre-History

Prior to the 1973-1974 school year, the RPI Pep Band was run by a salaried manager rather than by student managers. The one and only non-student manager was A. Olin Niles, the arranger of the “Hail, Dear Old Rensselaer” chart that the Pep Band still plays.

From a 12/2/81 issue of the Poly:

_“At its founding in the early 1920’s, the band had eight members and often had to hire professionals to complete an orchestra. Today, the band fields 76 pieces including 38 woodwinds, 32 brass, and 6 percussion instruments. The roots of the band can actually be traced back to 1923, when a local musician named A. Olin Niles organized the school’s second musical group (the Glee Club had been formed about 45 years earlier.) Mr. Niles had been performing in the pit of the American Theatre in the days of silent films. The President of the Union asked him to start a music program at the Institute, and Mr. Niles complied. As the talkies (modern movies) came into being, orchestras such as the one at the American became less popular and Niles was able to devote more time to the Engineer ensemble. In the early days, the band not only played at athletic events, but also gave concerts and played at dances. The group performed for the lacrosse, hockey, basketball and football teams, and would play not only the RPI school song, but also the alma mater of the opposing squad. In 1954, when the hockey team won the NCAA championship, the band took two busses and greeted them at the airport. Membership grew and through the years players broke off to form other musical groups. Niles, who was a big fan of the marches of Sousa, Goldman, and others, retired in 1973 after 50 years of service. Now 88 and living in Troy, he remains an avid fan of RPI sports.”_

**What Was It Like Back When We Had a Salaried Manager? (1960’s)**  
 (Thanks to George Harrison ’70 for these memories)

**Forward, March!**

During the 1960’s, RPI’s band was a marching band, in addition to being a pep band. Of course, it didn’t do any marching during hockey season, but it performed halftime marching routines at every home football game and participated in an occasional parade.

**Fight Song**

“[Hail, Dear Old Rensselaer](https://pepband.union.rpi.edu/music/LongHail.mp3)” was the fight song in the 1960’s, and it consisted, as it does today, of an introductory fanfare, an eight line refrain, a four line interlude, and a repeat of the eight line refrain. However, there were some differences in how it was performed.  
 The fight song used to be played noticeable more slowly than is the case today. Basically, the marching band of the ’60’s played the fight song at the same speed as that at which they marched. They would have worn out pretty quickly if they had tried to march at the tempo at which the fight song is played today.

In the 1960’s, the band would play the fanfare and the eight line refrain, as it does today, but would then sing the four line interlude, rather than playing it instrumentally. The only band members who played their instruments during that interlude were the drummers, who rattled through a drum solo during the line “Hear the rat-tat-tat of drums that beat.” After singing “Hear that might shout of”, the band members would bring their horns back up and play the refrain for the second and final time.

After Olin Niles’ retirement, there was a period of a year or two when the interlude was dropped entirely, so that the fight song consisted of the opening fanfare followed by the refrain being played twice straight through. Eventually, the interlude was restored as an instrumental version, and it has remained that way since.

At some point someone updated the words of the fight song to make it more politically correct than it was back in the 60’s. Now, the fourth line is “We all must do our part” and the fifth line is “True to old Rensselaer.” In the 60’s, the fourth line was “Each man must do his part” and the fifth line was “True sons of Rensselaer.” (Appallingly sexist, weren’t we?) I guess that, when a freshman entering class consisted of 1,001 males and 28 females, there was a tendency not to be as conscious as we ought to have been of the feminist point of view.

It was customary during that time, as it is today, for the band to play the fight song to salute the hockey team’s arrival on the ice at the start of the period, or the football team’s arrival on the field for the start of a half. While that was going on, it was also customary for all RPI fans to stand up and clap along in time with the music. Of course, the part about the fans standing up and clapping no longer holds true. I’m not sure just when that part of the tradition died out, although my recollection is that it continued at least through the hockey team’s NCAA championship season of 1984-85.  
[Alma Mater](https://pepband.union.rpi.edu/music/Alma%20Mater.mp3)

**Football**  
 The marching band’s halftime routine varied from game to game, but the ending was always the same. At the conclusion of the routine, the band would form an “R” and play the alma mater from that formation.

**Hockey**  
 At one time it was customary for the band to play the alma maters of both schools prior to the start of the thrid period of hockey games. (At least, they did so when they could get their hands on the sheet music for the other school’s alma mater.) This was done only partially as a gesture of goodwill toward the opponents. There was another underlying reason for this custom, which eventually resulted in an NCAA rule change.

As you may be aware, RPI’s hockey coach of the 1950’s and early 1960’s was Ned Harkness, after whom the field to the north of the Field House is named.

Harkness always put competitive teams on the ice, but for some reason he always seemed to have a problem recruiting a full roster for his teams. RPI usually dressed four or five players fewer than the rules allowed, which led to fatigue problems for the players late in games. Harkness was known for doing anything he could to offset this disadvantage.

During Harkness’ era, the third period would begin in the following manner. The band would salute RPI’s return to the ice with the traditional playing of the fight song. As is customary at all hockey games everywhere, the teams would skate a couple laps around the ice to warm up and then gather around to tap their goalies on the pads for luck. Then those players who were not starting the period would go to their benches, while the starters moved toward center ice for the face-off. Finally, just before the referee got ready to drop the puck, the Field House P.A. announcer would intone, “And now, the (name of the opponents) alma mater,” whereupon the band would play the visitor’ alma mater, followed by our own.

Eventually, opposing coaches figured out that, while this practice had the symbolic effect of showing respect for the visitors, it also had the very practical effect of giving Harkness’ chronically undermanned skaters several extra minutes of badly needed rest before starting the third period. After that, an NCAA rule was passed requiring that, if anybody’s band wants to play an alma mater, it has to do so before the teams return to the ice.

**Cheers**  
 The band today definitely has a larger variety of cheers than the band of the ’60’s. However, there are a couple from the 60’s that aren’t used today. The two cheers were pretty similar and both were used when it appeared that the referee had made a questionable call against RPI:

**Elevator Cheer**  
 Leader: “Elevator, elevator”  
 Band: “We got the shaft!”

**Carpenter Cheer**  
 Leader: “Carpenter, carpenter”  
 Band: “We got the screw!”  
 Mascot  
 What has the RPI band to do with the mascot, you ask? Well, the fact that RPI’s mascot today is NOT a white horse is, at least partly, due to the band.

In 1967, there was optimism that RPI’s football team might actually have a chance to beat our detested rivals from Union, who had beaten us n years in a row.

As the date of the game drew nigh, a Poly reporter, digging through the archives, discovered a reference to the fact that, once upon a time, RPI had had an official mascot, and that mascot had been a white horse. An article reporting on an RPI football game of many years before mentioned that the team had won as its good luck charm, “Otis,” the white horse, looked on beneficently from the sidelines.

In the hope that the return of its long-absent mascot might lend some inspiration to the football team, someone went out and rented a white horse from a local farmer for the Union game. Early arrivals at the ’86 field were treated to the sight of Otis, being held by a couple of students, standing near the northwest corner of the field.

The RPI band in those days was a marching band. It had been the custom for many years for the band to gather in front of the old student union building (now the Lally Management building) about 20-30 minutes prior to game time, then parade past the Troy and Ricketts Buildings and the ’87 gym on their way to their seats in the old grandstand, which stood on the south side of the field behind the RPI players’ bench. Although the current student union building at 15th and Sage had opened in the spring of 1967, the band still gathered in the traditional location in front of the old building to start its parade to the field.

As the band started its parade on the day of the Union game, with the drums beating and the horns playing, the horse, having never experienced anything like this in his placid agrarian existence, became increasingly agitated. By the time the band reached the Troy Building, Otis was spooked out of his mind. He began screaming, bucking, and rearing, until his handlers were finally obliged to lead him away, lest he injure himself or anybody else.

Thus deprived of whatever inspiration or good fortune Otis might have brought them, the Tute football team went out and got thrashed by Union for the n+1st year in a row. The white horse has never been seen at any RPI athletic event again.  
 Hey, Coach, Which End Do We Shoot At?  
 Nowadays, RPI’s hockey team shoots at the goal in front of the stage in the first and third periods. This wasn’t always the case. During the 1950’s and most of the ’60’s, it was traditional for RPI to shoot at the other end of the ice in the first and thrid periods. This remained the custom until the 1968-69 season, when Goalie Tom Nichol approached Coach Garry Kearns with a complaint.

Nichol said that, during the first and third periods of games, when he was defending the goal in front of the stage, he was constantly aware of the members of the band moving about, talking, and laughing on the stage behind him. Nichol felt that this distracted him from concentrating on the movement of the puck. He asked if the coach could speak to the band director and request that the band be quiet.

After thinking about it, the coach told Nichol that it was probably unrealistic to expect the band to sit there like a bunch of church mice all the time – after all, the band was entitled to have fun during the game, too.

But, Kearns went on, maybe the situation could be turned into an advantage. If the band was that much of a distraction to Nichol without meaning to be, think how much of a distraction it could be to the OTHER team’s goalie if HE had to play in front of the band two periods a game.

RPI immediately adopted the tradition of shooting at the stage end in the first and third periods. The current band follows in the footsteps of three decades’ worth of predecessors in making the lives of opposing goalies a little more miserable for two-thirds of each game.

1973-1974: Which We Only Heard About In Stories  
 For the quarterfinals of the ECAC playoffs of the ’73-’74 season, the Pep Band traveled to the University of New Hampshire where RPI won. For the semifinals and finals, the Pep Band traveled to Boston for two nights of playoff games at Boston Garden, where RPI lost to Harvard and Cornell.

1974-1975: Birth of the Modern Pep Band – We Were There

Senior Band Manager: Mike Popik, Class of ’73, Clarinet  
 Assistant Band Manager: Beth Montalone, Class of ’76, Flute

This was the first year that the RPI Pep Band was run by student managers and funded by the Student Union.

During the regular hockey season, the Pep Band traveled to Clarkson and St. Lawrence for the two-day North Trip.

This year, Basketball band was run by Ernie (a.k.a. “Tuba”) ?last name?, Class of ?, Sousaphone, and they traveled to Clarkson and St. Lawrence (by car) for a two-day road trip.

It was customary during that time, as it is today, for the band to play the fight song to salute the hockey team’s arrival on the ice at the start of the period, or the football team’s arrival on the field for the start of a half. While that was going on, it was also customary for all RPI fans to stand up and clap along in time with the music. Of course, the part about the fans standing up and clapping no longer holds true. I’m not sure just when that part of the tradition died out, although my recollection is that it continued at least through the hockey team’s NCAA championship season of 1984-85.  
[Alma Mater](https://pepband.union.rpi.edu/music/Alma%20Mater.mp3)

**Football**  
 The marching band’s halftime routine varied from game to game, but the ending was always the same. At the conclusion of the routine, the band would form an “R” and play the alma mater from that formation.

**Hockey**  
 At one time it was customary for the band to play the alma maters of both schools prior to the start of the thrid period of hockey games. (At least, they did so when they could get their hands on the sheet music for the other school’s alma mater.) This was done only partially as a gesture of goodwill toward the opponents. There was another underlying reason for this custom, which eventually resulted in an NCAA rule change.

As you may be aware, RPI’s hockey coach of the 1950’s and early 1960’s was Ned Harkness, after whom the field to the north of the Field House is named.

Harkness always put competitive teams on the ice, but for some reason he always seemed to have a problem recruiting a full roster for his teams. RPI usually dressed four or five players fewer than the rules allowed, which led to fatigue problems for the players late in games. Harkness was known for doing anything he could to offset this disadvantage.

During Harkness’ era, the third period would begin in the following manner. The band would salute RPI’s return to the ice with the traditional playing of the fight song. As is customary at all hockey games everywhere, the teams would skate a couple laps around the ice to warm up and then gather around to tap their goalies on the pads for luck. Then those players who were not starting the period would go to their benches, while the starters moved toward center ice for the face-off. Finally, just before the referee got ready to drop the puck, the Field House P.A. announcer would intone, “And now, the (name of the opponents) alma mater,” whereupon the band would play the visitor’ alma mater, followed by our own.

Eventually, opposing coaches figured out that, while this practice had the symbolic effect of showing respect for the visitors, it also had the very practical effect of giving Harkness’ chronically undermanned skaters several extra minutes of badly needed rest before starting the third period. After that, an NCAA rule was passed requiring that, if anybody’s band wants to play an alma mater, it has to do so before the teams return to the ice.

**Cheers**  
 The band today definitely has a larger variety of cheers than the band of the ’60’s. However, there are a couple from the 60’s that aren’t used today. The two cheers were pretty similar and both were used when it appeared that the referee had made a questionable call against RPI:

**Elevator Cheer**  
 Leader: “Elevator, elevator”  
 Band: “We got the shaft!”

**Carpenter Cheer**  
 Leader: “Carpenter, carpenter”  
 Band: “We got the screw!”  
 Mascot  
 What has the RPI band to do with the mascot, you ask? Well, the fact that RPI’s mascot today is NOT a white horse is, at least partly, due to the band.

In 1967, there was optimism that RPI’s football team might actually have a chance to beat our detested rivals from Union, who had beaten us n years in a row.

As the date of the game drew nigh, a Poly reporter, digging through the archives, discovered a reference to the fact that, once upon a time, RPI had had an official mascot, and that mascot had been a white horse. An article reporting on an RPI football game of many years before mentioned that the team had won as its good luck charm, “Otis,” the white horse, looked on beneficently from the sidelines.

In the hope that the return of its long-absent mascot might lend some inspiration to the football team, someone went out and rented a white horse from a local farmer for the Union game. Early arrivals at the ’86 field were treated to the sight of Otis, being held by a couple of students, standing near the northwest corner of the field.

The RPI band in those days was a marching band. It had been the custom for many years for the band to gather in front of the old student union building (now the Lally Management building) about 20-30 minutes prior to game time, then parade past the Troy and Ricketts Buildings and the ’87 gym on their way to their seats in the old grandstand, which stood on the south side of the field behind the RPI players’ bench. Although the current student union building at 15th and Sage had opened in the spring of 1967, the band still gathered in the traditional location in front of the old building to start its parade to the field.

As the band started its parade on the day of the Union game, with the drums beating and the horns playing, the horse, having never experienced anything like this in his placid agrarian existence, became increasingly agitated. By the time the band reached the Troy Building, Otis was spooked out of his mind. He began screaming, bucking, and rearing, until his handlers were finally obliged to lead him away, lest he injure himself or anybody else.

Thus deprived of whatever inspiration or good fortune Otis might have brought them, the Tute football team went out and got thrashed by Union for the n+1st year in a row. The white horse has never been seen at any RPI athletic event again.  
 Hey, Coach, Which End Do We Shoot At?  
 Nowadays, RPI’s hockey team shoots at the goal in front of the stage in the first and third periods. This wasn’t always the case. During the 1950’s and most of the ’60’s, it was traditional for RPI to shoot at the other end of the ice in the first and thrid periods. This remained the custom until the 1968-69 season, when Goalie Tom Nichol approached Coach Garry Kearns with a complaint.

Nichol said that, during the first and third periods of games, when he was defending the goal in front of the stage, he was constantly aware of the members of the band moving about, talking, and laughing on the stage behind him. Nichol felt that this distracted him from concentrating on the movement of the puck. He asked if the coach could speak to the band director and request that the band be quiet.

After thinking about it, the coach told Nichol that it was probably unrealistic to expect the band to sit there like a bunch of church mice all the time – after all, the band was entitled to have fun during the game, too.

But, Kearns went on, maybe the situation could be turned into an advantage. If the band was that much of a distraction to Nichol without meaning to be, think how much of a distraction it could be to the OTHER team’s goalie if HE had to play in front of the band two periods a game.

RPI immediately adopted the tradition of shooting at the stage end in the first and third periods. The current band follows in the footsteps of three decades’ worth of predecessors in making the lives of opposing goalies a little more miserable for two-thirds of each game.

# BAND PLAYING

During the eighteenth century, the term "band" was used in several European languages to describe military and civic ensembles that featured oboes, bassoons, and clarinets. Horns and trumpets were employed less frequently. Ensembles usually ranged from six to eight members.

As Europeans settled in the colonies, they brought band instruments with them. The first documented performance of a military band was in 1714, when oboes and trumpets were used to celebrate the crowning of [George I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/history/british-and-irish-history-biographies/george-i). The first documented civic concert of instrumental music took place in Boston in 1729. Moravian immigrants, well known for the importance they placed upon music, formed some of the first civilian bands in [North Carolina](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/north-carolina) and Pennsylvania.

## From Nationhood Through the [Civil War](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/ancient-greece-and-rome/ancient-history-rome/civil-war)

During the Revolutionary War, several American military bands were founded. The Third and Fourth Continental Artillery units had bands of exceptional renown. When state militia groups replaced the Continental Army in 1783, many of the militias formed small bands. They performed for ceremonial purposes and also at town dances and parades. In 1800, the U.S. Marine Corps established a permanent band that performed public concerts; this original band included two oboes, two clarinets, two horns, one bassoon, and one drum.

During the second decade of the nineteenth century, instrument makers developed valved brass instruments that were easier to play and more versatile. The keyed bugle was introduced in America in 1815 and enjoyed several decades of popularity. The bass drum and cymbal (which made their way into European and American ensembles through an enthusiasm for Turkish military, or "anissary" music) were gradually popularized. As a result, brass instruments quickly replaced woodwinds as the bands' basic element.

The [Civil War](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/ancient-greece-and-rome/ancient-history-rome/civil-war) saw the proliferation of many brass bands. Many militia bands enlisted as a group. The Union is estimated to have had 500 bands with 9,000 players. These bands consisted of anywhere from eight to twenty-four musicians.

## The Rise of Amateur Band Playing

After the Civil War there was a dramatic rise in amateur band playing. Instruments became more affordable as American manufacturing replaced the importation of instruments from Europe; in addition, instrument quality increased. Both brass and woodwind instruments were sold in high quantities, reversing the previous trend toward the exclusive use of brass instruments. Local manufacturers implemented massive advertising campaigns that emphasized the positive effects of playing in a band: the health benefits of marching, the fact that women found bandsmen more attractive, and the ability of a band to draw a crowd for political or commercial reasons.

Amateur bands were funded and organized by a number of institutions. Many town governments funded bands, arguing that the presence of a town band reflected the town's high level of taste and civilization. Fraternal and sororital organizations formed bands, pointing to the positive moral influence of band playing. Bands were also formed around industrial ties (such as factory bands and railroad bands), by the [Salvation Army](https://www.encyclopedia.com/philosophy-and-religion/christianity/protestant-denominations/salvation-army) (in 1878), and (after [World War I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/wars-and-battles/world-war-i)) by [American Legion](https://www.encyclopedia.com/sports-and-everyday-life/social-organizations/private-organizations/american-legion) posts and veterans' organizations. Bands were conducted by local music "professors" and rehearsed once or twice a week. Membership was generally restricted to adult males, though a small number of women's bands were formed around 1900. The standard size of a band rose steadily, peaking at about twenty members.

## Role of Bands in Town Life

From 1850 to [World War I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/wars-and-battles/world-war-i) (often called "the golden age of bands"), bands could be found in almost every town in America. In most communities, bands provided the main source of music outside the home. Bands performed a wide repertoire of music, from marches and dance music to arrangements of everything from the latest opera aria to Stephen Foster songs to European symphonic literature. They performed at paid political rallies, fairs, parades, picnics, and excursions. During the summer months, bands would perform at unpaid summer evening concerts once a week at the town bandstand. These events in the center of town drew large crowds.

During this period, rivalry between bands was high. Community bands fought to recruit the best players, and bands worked hard to have the most appealing repertoire, the best instruments, and the most exotic costumes. During the 1870s and 1880s, instrument manufacturers and chambers of commerce often staged competitions. Several of these competitions reached mammoth proportions, lasting three to four days and drawing crowds from great distances.

## The Origins and Development of Band Playing in Schools

While the number of civic bands has sharply declined since World War I, bands can now be found in most educational institutions across America. The University of Notre Dame Band, formed in 1842, claims to be the oldest band in continuous existence. After the Civil War, bands were formed at the Officer's Training Corps, which could be found at most [colleges and universities](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/education/education-terms-and-concepts/colleges-and-universities). The combination of military training and music making converged in the marching band, which, in the early 2000s, remained the most prominent type of school band. By 1900, it was common to have bands performing at half-time shows of sporting events.

The end of World War I saw many military band-leaders return to their communities and form bands in public high schools. These bands benefited from the increasing tendency toward publicly funded music instruction. Their popularity was also fueled by intense competition. In 1923, in a bid to increase sales, musical instrument manufacturers sponsored the first national school band contest. Organizations for the promotion of school bands were founded: the National School Band Association in 1926, the College Band Directors National Association in 1941.

Recent years have seen the rise of "wind ensembles" in many universities and colleges. This trend began in 1952 with the foundation of the Eastman School of Music Symphonic Wind Ensemble by Frederic Fennell. Wind ensembles generally have fewer members than bands, and their instrumentation is modeled on the symphony orchestra. These ensembles attempt to rival the symphony orchestra in terms of virtuosity, sophistication, and versatility.

# BAND PLAYING

During the eighteenth century, the term "band" was used in several European languages to describe military and civic ensembles that featured oboes, bassoons, and clarinets. Horns and trumpets were employed less frequently. Ensembles usually ranged from six to eight members.

As Europeans settled in the colonies, they brought band instruments with them. The first documented performance of a military band was in 1714, when oboes and trumpets were used to celebrate the crowning of [George I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/history/british-and-irish-history-biographies/george-i). The first documented civic concert of instrumental music took place in Boston in 1729. Moravian immigrants, well known for the importance they placed upon music, formed some of the first civilian bands in [North Carolina](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/north-carolina) and Pennsylvania.

## From Nationhood Through the [Civil War](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/ancient-greece-and-rome/ancient-history-rome/civil-war)

During the Revolutionary War, several American military bands were founded. The Third and Fourth Continental Artillery units had bands of exceptional renown. When state militia groups replaced the Continental Army in 1783, many of the militias formed small bands. They performed for ceremonial purposes and also at town dances and parades. In 1800, the U.S. Marine Corps established a permanent band that performed public concerts; this original band included two oboes, two clarinets, two horns, one bassoon, and one drum.

During the second decade of the nineteenth century, instrument makers developed valved brass instruments that were easier to play and more versatile. The keyed bugle was introduced in America in 1815 and enjoyed several decades of popularity. The bass drum and cymbal (which made their way into European and American ensembles through an enthusiasm for Turkish military, or "anissary" music) were gradually popularized. As a result, brass instruments quickly replaced woodwinds as the bands' basic element.

The [Civil War](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/ancient-greece-and-rome/ancient-history-rome/civil-war) saw the proliferation of many brass bands. Many militia bands enlisted as a group. The Union is estimated to have had 500 bands with 9,000 players. These bands consisted of anywhere from eight to twenty-four musicians.

## The Rise of Amateur Band Playing

After the Civil War there was a dramatic rise in amateur band playing. Instruments became more affordable as American manufacturing replaced the importation of instruments from Europe; in addition, instrument quality increased. Both brass and woodwind instruments were sold in high quantities, reversing the previous trend toward the exclusive use of brass instruments. Local manufacturers implemented massive advertising campaigns that emphasized the positive effects of playing in a band: the health benefits of marching, the fact that women found bandsmen more attractive, and the ability of a band to draw a crowd for political or commercial reasons.

Amateur bands were funded and organized by a number of institutions. Many town governments funded bands, arguing that the presence of a town band reflected the town's high level of taste and civilization. Fraternal and sororital organizations formed bands, pointing to the positive moral influence of band playing. Bands were also formed around industrial ties (such as factory bands and railroad bands), by the [Salvation Army](https://www.encyclopedia.com/philosophy-and-religion/christianity/protestant-denominations/salvation-army) (in 1878), and (after [World War I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/wars-and-battles/world-war-i)) by [American Legion](https://www.encyclopedia.com/sports-and-everyday-life/social-organizations/private-organizations/american-legion) posts and veterans' organizations. Bands were conducted by local music "professors" and rehearsed once or twice a week. Membership was generally restricted to adult males, though a small number of women's bands were formed around 1900. The standard size of a band rose steadily, peaking at about twenty members.

## Role of Bands in Town Life

From 1850 to [World War I](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/wars-and-battles/world-war-i) (often called "the golden age of bands"), bands could be found in almost every town in America. In most communities, bands provided the main source of music outside the home. Bands performed a wide repertoire of music, from marches and dance music to arrangements of everything from the latest opera aria to Stephen Foster songs to European symphonic literature. They performed at paid political rallies, fairs, parades, picnics, and excursions. During the summer months, bands would perform at unpaid summer evening concerts once a week at the town bandstand. These events in the center of town drew large crowds.

During this period, rivalry between bands was high. Community bands fought to recruit the best players, and bands worked hard to have the most appealing repertoire, the best instruments, and the most exotic costumes. During the 1870s and 1880s, instrument manufacturers and chambers of commerce often staged competitions. Several of these competitions reached mammoth proportions, lasting three to four days and drawing crowds from great distances.

## The Origins and Development of Band Playing in Schools

While the number of civic bands has sharply declined since World War I, bands can now be found in most educational institutions across America. The University of Notre Dame Band, formed in 1842, claims to be the oldest band in continuous existence. After the Civil War, bands were formed at the Officer's Training Corps, which could be found at most [colleges and universities](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/education/education-terms-and-concepts/colleges-and-universities). The combination of military training and music making converged in the marching band, which, in the early 2000s, remained the most prominent type of school band. By 1900, it was common to have bands performing at half-time shows of sporting events.

The end of World War I saw many military band-leaders return to their communities and form bands in public high schools. These bands benefited from the increasing tendency toward publicly funded music instruction. Their popularity was also fueled by intense competition. In 1923, in a bid to increase sales, musical instrument manufacturers sponsored the first national school band contest. Organizations for the promotion of school bands were founded: the National School Band Association in 1926, the College Band Directors National Association in 1941.

Recent years have seen the rise of "wind ensembles" in many universities and colleges. This trend began in 1952 with the foundation of the Eastman School of Music Symphonic Wind Ensemble by Frederic Fennell. Wind ensembles generally have fewer members than bands, and their instrumentation is modeled on the symphony orchestra. These ensembles attempt to rival the symphony orchestra in terms of virtuosity, sophistication, and versatility.

**Yes** are an English [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock") band formed in London in 1968. Having featured [20 full-time musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_band_members "List of Yes band members") across their history, their most notable members include lead singer [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"), bassist [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire"), guitarists [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe") and [Trevor Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Rabin "Trevor Rabin"), drummers [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford") and [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)"), and keyboardists [Tony Kaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Kaye_(musician) "Tony Kaye (musician)") and [Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Wakeman "Rick Wakeman"), who represented Yes when they were inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 2017. Widely regarded as progressive rock pioneers, the group have explored several musical styles and remain one of the most successful, influential, and longest-lasting acts in the genre. [Their discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_discography "Yes discography") spans 25 studio albums, with 13.5 million [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA)-certified albums sold in the United States[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-riaatotal-1) and more than 30 million worldwide.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-2)

Founded by Anderson, Squire, Bruford, Kaye, and guitarist [Peter Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Banks "Peter Banks"), Yes began performing a mix of original songs and covers spanning rock, pop, blues, and jazz, as showcased on their first two albums, _[Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes\_(Yes\_album) "Yes (Yes album)")_ (1969) and _[Time and a Word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_and\_a\_Word "Time and a Word")_ (1970). A change of direction in 1970 following the replacement of Banks with Howe led to a series of celebrated progressive rock albums, including four consecutive US platinum or multi-platinum sellers: _[The Yes Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Yes\_Album "The Yes Album")_ (1971); _[Fragile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fragile\_(Yes\_album) "Fragile (Yes album)")_ (1971), which included the hit single "[Roundabout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundabout_(song) "Roundabout (song)")"; _[Close to the Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close\_to\_the\_Edge "Close to the Edge")_ (1972); and the live album _[Yessongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yessongs "Yessongs")_ (1973). Subsequent releases, including _[Tales from Topographic Oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Topographic\_Oceans "Tales from Topographic Oceans")_ (1973), _[Going for the One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Going\_for\_the\_One "Going for the One")_ (1977), and _[Tormato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tormato "Tormato")_ (1978), also achieved major commercial success. Yes earned a reputation for their elaborate stage sets, light displays, and iconic album covers designed by [Roger Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Dean_(artist) "Roger Dean (artist)"). Personnel shifted frequently during this era; following the 1980 departures of Anderson and Wakeman, Yes recruited keyboardist [Geoff Downes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Downes "Geoff Downes") and singer [Trevor Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Horn "Trevor Horn") of [the Buggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Buggles "The Buggles") for the album _[Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama\_(Yes\_album) "Drama (Yes album)")_ (1980) before the group dissolved the following year.

In 1983, Squire, White, Anderson, Kaye, and Rabin reformed Yes. Rabin's songwriting moved the group toward a mainstream pop-rock sound, resulting in their highest-selling album, _[90125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90125\_(album) "90125 (album)")_ (1983). This release featured the group's only US number-one single, "[Owner of a Lonely Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owner_of_a_Lonely_Heart "Owner of a Lonely Heart")", and won a [Grammy Award for Best Rock Instrumental Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rock_Instrumental_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Rock Instrumental Performance") for the track "[Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_(Yes_song) "Cinema (Yes song)")". The follow-up album, _[Big Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Generator "Big Generator")_ (1987), was also successful. In 1989, the offshoot group [Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anderson_Bruford_Wakeman_Howe "Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe") formed and released a self-titled album. At the suggestion of their record company, both factions merged into a short-lived eight-piece line-up for _[Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union\_(Yes\_album) "Union (Yes album)")_ (1991) and its corresponding tour. Yes continued to tour regularly and release albums—including the symphonically backed _[Magnification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnification\_(album) "Magnification (album)")_ (2001)—before entering a temporary hiatus in 2004.

Following the cancellation of a 2008 tour due to Anderson's health, Yes enlisted [Benoît David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_David "Benoît David") as their new lead singer and resumed activity. [Jon Davison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Davison "Jon Davison") replaced David in 2012. Squire died in 2015, leaving the band with no remaining original members. Three former members toured separately as [Yes Featuring Jon Anderson, Trevor Rabin, Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_Featuring_Jon_Anderson,_Trevor_Rabin,_Rick_Wakeman "Yes Featuring Jon Anderson, Trevor Rabin, Rick Wakeman") from 2016 to 2018. White, the longest-tenured member at the time, died in 2022. Since February 2023, the band's line-up has consisted of Howe, Downes, Davison, bassist [Billy Sherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Sherwood "Billy Sherwood"), and drummer [Jay Schellen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Schellen "Jay Schellen"). Their latest studio album, _[Aurora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora\_(Yes\_album) "Aurora (Yes album)")_, was released in June 2026.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 1968–1970: Formation, first album and _Time and a Word_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1968–1970: Formation, first album and Time and a Word")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Yes_plaque_Basement_184_Shaftesbury_Avenue_London_WC2_8JB.jpg/250px-Yes_plaque_Basement_184_Shaftesbury_Avenue_London_WC2_8JB.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_plaque_Basement_184_Shaftesbury_Avenue_London_WC2_8JB.jpg)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Yes_the_English_Progressive_Rock_Band_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Yes_the_English_Progressive_Rock_Band_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_the_English_Progressive_Rock_Band_(cropped).jpg)

Yes formed in the basement of the Lucky Horseshoe Cafe (left) at 184 [Shaftesbury Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaftesbury_Avenue "Shaftesbury Avenue"), London in mid-1968. Right: commemorative plaque at the address.

In late 1967, bassist [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire") and guitarist [Peter Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Banks "Peter Banks"), both formerly of [the Syn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Syn "The Syn"), joined the [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") band [Mabel Greer's Toyshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabel_Greer's_Toyshop "Mabel Greer's Toyshop"), which had been formed in 1966 by Clive Bayley and Robert Hagger.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-Loudersound2014-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-ZM2015-4) They played at the [Marquee Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquee_Club "Marquee Club") in [Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho "Soho"), London where Jack Barrie, owner of the nearby La Chasse club, saw them perform.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200823-5) He later recalled: "the musicianship was very good but it was obvious they weren't going anywhere".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200823-5) Barrie introduced Squire to singer [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"), a worker at the bar in La Chasse, who found they shared interests in [Simon & Garfunkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Garfunkel "Simon & Garfunkel") and harmony singing. That evening they wrote "Sweetness", which was included on the first Yes album, and Anderson joined as lead vocalist.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200824-6) During this time, the band rehearsed in the basement of The Lucky Horseshoe cafe on [Shaftesbury Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaftesbury_Avenue "Shaftesbury Avenue") between 10 June and 9 July 1968.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruford200935-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200839-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200844-9) In June 1968, Hagger was replaced by [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford"), who had placed an advertisement in _[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody\_Maker "Melody Maker")_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200833%E2%80%9334-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200837-11) while in July the classically trained organist and pianist [Tony Kaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Kaye_(musician) "Tony Kaye (musician)"), of Johnny Taylor's Star Combo and the Federals, became the keyboardist.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200838-12) Meanwhile, Banks had left Mabel Greer's Toyshop to join Neat Change, but he was dismissed by this group on 14 July 1968[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200833%E2%80%9334-10) and was recalled by Squire, replacing Bayley as guitarist.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200833%E2%80%9334-10)

Having considered the experience of Mabel Greer's Toyshop concluded, the group exchanged ideas for a new name. Sources disagree on the origin of the name, but generally attribute it to Banks.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-Hunter-Tilney-2018-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-14)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200833%E2%80%9334-10) According to the _Financial Times_, Anderson suggested "Life" and Squire thought of "World"; Banks said simply, "Yes", and that was how the band was named.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-Hunter-Tilney-2018-13) Welch states that Squire suggested the name over a phone call to Banks, with Banks replying, "But that was my idea!"[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200833%E2%80%9334-10) According to Banks, it was initially used as a temporary name, but "nobody has thought of anything better yet."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200833%E2%80%9334-10)

After rehearsals between 31 July and 2 August, the first gig as Yes followed at a youth camp in [East Mersea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Mersea "East Mersea"), Essex on 3 August.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008op._cit.-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-16) Early sets were formed of cover songs from artists such as [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"), [The 5th Dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_5th_Dimension "The 5th Dimension") and [Traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_(band) "Traffic (band)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200845-17) On 16 September, Yes performed at Blaise's club in London as a substitute for [Sly and the Family Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_and_the_Family_Stone "Sly and the Family Stone"), who had failed to turn up. They were well received by the audience, including the host [Roy Flynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Flynn "Roy Flynn"), who became the band's manager that night.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200850%E2%80%9351-18) That month, Bruford decided to quit performing to study at the [University of Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leeds "University of Leeds").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200852%E2%80%9353-19) His replacement, Tony O'Reilly of [the Koobas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Koobas "The Koobas"), struggled to perform with the rest of the group on stage and former [Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Warriors_(British_band) "The Warriors (British band)") and future [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") drummer [Ian Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Wallace_(drummer) "Ian Wallace (drummer)") subbed for one gig on 5 November 1968.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200852%E2%80%9353-19) After Bruford was refused a year's sabbatical leave from Leeds, Anderson and Squire convinced him to return for Yes's supporting slot for [Cream's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cream_(band) "Cream (band)") farewell concert at the [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall") on 26 November.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200852%E2%80%9353-19)

After seeing an early [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") gig in 1969, Yes realised that there was suddenly stiff competition on the London gigging circuit, and they needed to be much more technically proficient, starting regular rehearsals.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-banks-20) They subsequently signed a deal with [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"), and, that August, released their debut album _[Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes\_(Yes\_album) "Yes (Yes album)")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008315-21) Compiled of mostly original material, the record includes renditions of "[Every Little Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Every_Little_Thing_(Beatles_song) "Every Little Thing (Beatles song)")" by the Beatles and "I See You" by [The Byrds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Byrds "The Byrds"). Although the album failed to break into the UK album charts, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ critic [Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs") complimented the album's "sense of style, taste and subtlety".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-22)_Melody Maker_ columnist Tony Wilson chose Yes and [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin") as the two bands "most likely to succeed".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-23)

Following a tour of Scandinavia with [Faces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faces_(band) "Faces (band)"), Yes performed a solo concert at the [Queen Elizabeth Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_Hall "Queen Elizabeth Hall") on 21 March 1970. The second half consisted of excerpts from their second album _[Time and a Word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_and\_a\_Word "Time and a Word")_, accompanied by a 20-piece youth orchestra.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200877-24) Banks left the group on 18 April 1970, just three months before the album's release. Having expressed dissatisfaction with the idea of recording with an orchestra as well as the sacking of Flynn earlier in the year,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008315-21)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200880-25) Banks later indicated that he was fired by Anderson and Squire, and that Kaye and Bruford had no prior knowledge that it would be happening.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-banks-20) Similar to the first album, _Time and a Word_ features original songs and two new covers–"Everydays" by [Buffalo Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Springfield "Buffalo Springfield") and "No Opportunity Necessary, No Experience Needed" by [Richie Havens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richie_Havens "Richie Havens"). The album broke into the UK charts, peaking at number 45.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) Banks' replacement was [Tomorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_(band) "Tomorrow (band)") guitarist [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe"), who appears in the photograph of the group on the American issue despite not having played on it.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch200889-27)

### 1970–1974: _The Yes Album_, _Fragile_, _Close to the Edge_ and _Tales from Topographic Oceans_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1970–1974: The Yes Album, Fragile, Close to the Edge and Tales from Topographic Oceans")]

The band retreated to a rented farmhouse in [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon") to write and rehearse new songs for their following album.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-28) Howe established himself as an integral part of the group's sound with his [Gibson ES-175](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibson_ES-175 "Gibson ES-175") and variety of acoustic guitars. With producer and engineer [Eddy Offord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Offord "Eddy Offord"), recording sessions lasted as long as 12 hours with each track being assembled from small sections at a time, which were pieced together to form a complete track. The band would then learn to play the song through after the final mix was complete.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-29) Released in February 1971, _[The Yes Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Yes\_Album "The Yes Album")_ peaked at number 4 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 40 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") charts.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Yes_1972_press_photo.jpg/250px-Yes_1972_press_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_1972_press_photo.jpg)

Yes in 1972. Standing: [Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Wakeman "Rick Wakeman") and [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe"). Seated: [Bill Bruford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Bruford "Bill Bruford") and [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"). Bottom: [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire").

Yes embarked on a 28-day tour of Europe with [Iron Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Butterfly "Iron Butterfly") in January 1971.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008102-31) The band purchased Iron Butterfly's entire [public address system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_address_system "Public address system"), which improved their on-stage performance and sound.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008104-32) Their first date in North America followed on 24 June in [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), Alberta, Canada, supporting [Jethro Tull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jethro_Tull_(band) "Jethro Tull (band)").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruford200955-33) Friction arose between Howe and Kaye on tour;[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008109-34) this, along with Kaye's reported reluctance to play the [Mellotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellotron "Mellotron") and the [Minimoog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog "Minimoog") synthesizer, preferring to stick exclusively to [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano") and [Hammond organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-NME_Rock_'N'_Roll_Years-35) led to the keyboardist being fired from the band in the summer of 1971. Anderson recalled in a 2019 interview: "Steve and Chris came over and said, 'Look, Tony Kaye... great guy.' But, you know, we'd just seen [Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Wakeman "Rick Wakeman") about a month earlier. And I said, 'There's that Rick Wakeman guy,' and we've got to get on with life and move on, you know, rather than keep going on, set in the same circle. And that's what happens with a band."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-BCBYesIndeed-36) Wakeman, a classically trained player who had left the folk rock group [Strawbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawbs "Strawbs") earlier in the year, was already a noted studio musician, with credits including [T. Rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Rex_(band) "T. Rex (band)"), [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"), [Cat Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_Stevens "Cat Stevens") and [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John"). Squire commented that he could play "a grand piano for three bars, a Mellotron for two bars and a Moog for the next one absolutely spot on",[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-37) which gave Yes the orchestral and choral textures that befitted their new material.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Released on 12 November 1971,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-38) the band's fourth album _[Fragile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fragile\_(Yes\_album) "Fragile (Yes album)")_ showcased their growing interest in the structures of classical music, with an excerpt of _[The Firebird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Firebird "The Firebird")_ by [Igor Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Stravinsky "Igor Stravinsky") being played at the start of their concerts since the album's [1971–1972 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fragile_Tour "Fragile Tour").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-39) Each member performed a solo track on the album, and it marked the start of their long collaboration with artist [Roger Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Dean_(artist) "Roger Dean (artist)"), who designed the [group's logo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_bubble_logo "Yes bubble logo"), album art and stage sets. _Fragile_ peaked at number 7 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 4 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) after it was released there in January 1972, and was their first record to reach the top ten in North America. A shorter version of the opening track, "[Roundabout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundabout_(Yes_song) "Roundabout (Yes song)")", was released as a single that peaked at number 13 on the _Billboard_[Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") singles chart.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40)

In February 1972, Yes recorded a cover version of "[America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America_(Simon_&_Garfunkel_song) "America (Simon & Garfunkel song)")" by [Simon & Garfunkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Garfunkel "Simon & Garfunkel") and released it in July. The single reached number 46 on the US singles chart.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) The track subsequently appeared on _[The New Age of Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Age\_of\_Atlantic "The New Age of Atlantic")_, a 1972 compilation album of several bands signed to Atlantic Records, and again in the 1975 compilation _[Yesterdays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesterdays\_(Yes\_album) "Yesterdays (Yes album)")_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-41)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Yes_1973_press_photo.jpg/250px-Yes_1973_press_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_1973_press_photo.jpg)

Yes in 1973. Clockwise from top left: Squire, Anderson, Wakeman, Howe and [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)").

Released in September 1972, _[Close to the Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close\_to\_the\_Edge "Close to the Edge")_, the band's fifth album, was their most ambitious work so far. At 19 minutes, the [title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_to_the_Edge_(song) "Close to the Edge (song)") took up an entire side on the vinyl record and combined elements of classical music, psychedelic rock, pop and jazz. The album reached number 3 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) and number 4 on the UK charts.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008185-42) "[And You and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_You_and_I "And You and I")" was released as a single that peaked at number 42 in the US[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) The growing critical and commercial success of the band was not enough to retain Bruford, who left Yes in the summer of 1972, before the album's release, to join [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson"). The band considered several possible replacements, including [Aynsley Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aynsley_Dunbar "Aynsley Dunbar") (who was playing with [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") at the time),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-43) and decided on former [Plastic Ono Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_Ono_Band "Plastic Ono Band") drummer [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)"), a friend of Anderson and Offord who had once sat in with the band weeks before Bruford's departure.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-44) White learned the band's repertoire in three days before embarking on their [1972–1973 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_to_the_Edge_Tour "Close to the Edge Tour").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-45)

By this point, Yes were beginning to enjoy worldwide commercial and critical success. Their early touring with White was featured on _[Yessongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yessongs "Yessongs")_, a triple live album released in May 1973 that documented shows from 1972. The album reached number 7 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 12 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008136-46) A [concert film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yessongs_(film) "Yessongs (film)") of the same name premiered in 1975[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008146-47) that documented their shows at London's [Rainbow Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Theatre "Rainbow Theatre") in December 1972.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorse199642-48)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Rick_Wakeman_-_Winterland_1974.jpg/250px-Rick_Wakeman_-_Winterland_1974.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rick_Wakeman_-_Winterland_1974.jpg)

Rick Wakeman with Yes in March 1974, months before his first departure from the band

> It is a fragmented masterpiece, assembled with loving care and long hours in the studio. Brilliant in patches, but often taking far too long to make its various points, and curiously lacking in warmth or personal expression ..."Ritual" is a dance of celebration and brings the first enjoyable moments, where Alan's driving drums have something to grip on to and the lyrics of la la la speak volumes. But even this cannot last long and cohesion is lost once more to the gods of drab self indulgence.

—_[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody\_Maker "Melody Maker")_ review of _[Tales from Topographic Oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Topographic\_Oceans "Tales from Topographic Oceans")_, 1973[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-Melody_Maker_TFTO-49)

_[Tales from Topographic Oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Topographic\_Oceans "Tales from Topographic Oceans")_ was the band's sixth studio album, released on 7 December 1973.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-50) It marked a change in their fortunes and polarised fans and critics alike. The double vinyl set was based on Anderson's interpretation of the [Shastric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shastra "Shastra") scriptures from a footnote within [Paramahansa Yogananda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramahansa_Yogananda "Paramahansa Yogananda")'s book _[Autobiography of a Yogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiography\_of\_a\_Yogi "Autobiography of a Yogi")_. The album became the first LP in the UK to ship gold before the record arrived at retailers.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-51) It went on to [top the UK charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UK_Albums_Chart_number_ones_of_the_1970s#1974 "List of UK Albums Chart number ones of the 1970s") for two weeks[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) while reaching number 6 in the US,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) and became the band's fourth consecutive gold album. Wakeman was not pleased with the record and is critical of much of its material.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-spinal-52) He felt sections were "bled to death" and contained too much musical padding.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-53) Wakeman left the band after the [1973–1974 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales_from_Topographic_Oceans_Tour "Tales from Topographic Oceans Tour"); his solo album _[Journey to the Centre of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey\_to\_the\_Centre\_of\_the\_Earth\_(album) "Journey to the Centre of the Earth (album)")_ topped the UK charts in May 1974.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-54) The tour included five consecutive sold-out shows at the Rainbow Theatre, the first time a rock band achieved this.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWooding1978114-55)

### 1974–1980: _Relayer_, _Going for the One_, _Tormato_ and the Paris sessions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1974–1980: Relayer, Going for the One, Tormato and the Paris sessions")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Yes_%28Anderson%2C_Squire%2C_Howe%2C_White%2C_Moraz%29.jpg/250px-Yes_%28Anderson%2C_Squire%2C_Howe%2C_White%2C_Moraz%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_(Anderson,_Squire,_Howe,_White,_Moraz).jpg)

Yes in 1974. Left to right: [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe"), [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"), [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire"), [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)"), and [Patrick Moraz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Moraz "Patrick Moraz")

Several musicians were approached to replace Wakeman, including [Vangelis Papathanassiou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vangelis_Papathanassiou "Vangelis Papathanassiou"), [Eddie Jobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Jobson "Eddie Jobson") of [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music") and former Atlantis/Cat Stevens keyboardist [Jean Roussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Roussel "Jean Roussel"). Howe says he also asked [Keith Emerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Emerson "Keith Emerson"), who did not want to leave [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2021108-56) Yes ultimately chose Swiss keyboardist [Patrick Moraz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Moraz "Patrick Moraz") of [Refugee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_(band) "Refugee (band)"), who arrived in August 1974[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-57) during the recording sessions for _[Relayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relayer "Relayer")_, which took place at Squire's home in [Virginia Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Water "Virginia Water"), Surrey. Released in November that year, _Relayer_ showcased a [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion")-influenced direction the band were pursuing. The album features the 22-minute track titled "[The Gates of Delirium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gates_of_Delirium "The Gates of Delirium")", which highlights a battle initially inspired by _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ by [Leo Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy "Leo Tolstoy"). Its closing section, "Soon", was subsequently released as a single. The album reached No. 4 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and No. 5 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008154-58) Yes embarked on their [1974–1975 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1960s%E2%80%9370s)#Relayer_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1960s–70s)") to support _Relayer_. The compilation album _[Yesterdays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesterdays\_(Yes\_album) "Yesterdays (Yes album)")_, released in 1975, contained tracks from Yes's first two albums, the B-side track from their "Sweet Dreams" single from 1970 titled "Dear Father", and the original ten-minute version of their cover of "America".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-59)

Between 1975 and 1976, each member of the band released a solo album. Their subsequent [1976 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1960s%E2%80%9370s)#1976_Solo_Albums_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1960s–70s)") of North America with [Peter Frampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Frampton "Peter Frampton") featured some of the band's most-attended shows. The show of 12 June, also supported by [Gary Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Wright "Gary Wright") and [Pousette-Dart Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pousette-Dart_Band "Pousette-Dart Band") at [John F. Kennedy Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_Stadium_(Philadelphia) "John F. Kennedy Stadium (Philadelphia)") in Philadelphia, attracted over 100,000 people.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-60) Roger Dean's brother Martyn was the main designer behind the tour's "Crab Nebula" stage set, while Roger and fabric designer Felicity Youette provided the backgrounds.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Yes_concert.jpg/250px-Yes_concert.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_concert.jpg)

Yes in concert in August 1977. From left to right: [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe"), [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)") (behind the drums), [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"), [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire") and [Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Wakeman "Rick Wakeman").
