The single reached number 46 on the US singles chart.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) The track subsequently appeared on _[The New Age of Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Age\_of\_Atlantic "The New Age of Atlantic")_, a 1972 compilation album of several bands signed to Atlantic Records, and again in the 1975 compilation _[Yesterdays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesterdays\_(Yes\_album) "Yesterdays (Yes album)")_.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-41)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Yes_1973_press_photo.jpg/250px-Yes_1973_press_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_1973_press_photo.jpg)

Yes in 1973. Clockwise from top left: Squire, Anderson, Wakeman, Howe and [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)").

Released in September 1972, _[Close to the Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close\_to\_the\_Edge "Close to the Edge")_, the band's fifth album, was their most ambitious work so far. At 19 minutes, the [title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_to_the_Edge_(song) "Close to the Edge (song)") took up an entire side on the vinyl record and combined elements of classical music, psychedelic rock, pop and jazz. The album reached number 3 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) and number 4 on the UK charts.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008185-42) "[And You and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_You_and_I "And You and I")" was released as a single that peaked at number 42 in the US[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) The growing critical and commercial success of the band was not enough to retain Bruford, who left Yes in the summer of 1972, before the album's release, to join [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson"). The band considered several possible replacements, including [Aynsley Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aynsley_Dunbar "Aynsley Dunbar") (who was playing with [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa") at the time),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-43) and decided on former [Plastic Ono Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_Ono_Band "Plastic Ono Band") drummer [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)"), a friend of Anderson and Offord who had once sat in with the band weeks before Bruford's departure.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-44) White learned the band's repertoire in three days before embarking on their [1972–1973 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_to_the_Edge_Tour "Close to the Edge Tour").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-45)

By this point, Yes were beginning to enjoy worldwide commercial and critical success. Their early touring with White was featured on _[Yessongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yessongs "Yessongs")_, a triple live album released in May 1973 that documented shows from 1972. The album reached number 7 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 12 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008136-46) A [concert film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yessongs_(film) "Yessongs (film)") of the same name premiered in 1975[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008146-47) that documented their shows at London's [Rainbow Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Theatre "Rainbow Theatre") in December 1972.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorse199642-48)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Rick_Wakeman_-_Winterland_1974.jpg/250px-Rick_Wakeman_-_Winterland_1974.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rick_Wakeman_-_Winterland_1974.jpg)

Rick Wakeman with Yes in March 1974, months before his first departure from the band

> It is a fragmented masterpiece, assembled with loving care and long hours in the studio. Brilliant in patches, but often taking far too long to make its various points, and curiously lacking in warmth or personal expression ..."Ritual" is a dance of celebration and brings the first enjoyable moments, where Alan's driving drums have something to grip on to and the lyrics of la la la speak volumes. But even this cannot last long and cohesion is lost once more to the gods of drab self indulgence.

—_[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody\_Maker "Melody Maker")_ review of _[Tales from Topographic Oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Topographic\_Oceans "Tales from Topographic Oceans")_, 1973[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-Melody_Maker_TFTO-49)

_[Tales from Topographic Oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_from\_Topographic\_Oceans "Tales from Topographic Oceans")_ was the band's sixth studio album, released on 7 December 1973.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-50) It marked a change in their fortunes and polarised fans and critics alike. The double vinyl set was based on Anderson's interpretation of the [Shastric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shastra "Shastra") scriptures from a footnote within [Paramahansa Yogananda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramahansa_Yogananda "Paramahansa Yogananda")'s book _[Autobiography of a Yogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiography\_of\_a\_Yogi "Autobiography of a Yogi")_. The album became the first LP in the UK to ship gold before the record arrived at retailers.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-51) It went on to [top the UK charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UK_Albums_Chart_number_ones_of_the_1970s#1974 "List of UK Albums Chart number ones of the 1970s") for two weeks[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) while reaching number 6 in the US,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) and became the band's fourth consecutive gold album. Wakeman was not pleased with the record and is critical of much of its material.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-spinal-52) He felt sections were "bled to death" and contained too much musical padding.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-53) Wakeman left the band after the [1973–1974 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales_from_Topographic_Oceans_Tour "Tales from Topographic Oceans Tour"); his solo album _[Journey to the Centre of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey\_to\_the\_Centre\_of\_the\_Earth\_(album) "Journey to the Centre of the Earth (album)")_ topped the UK charts in May 1974.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-54) The tour included five consecutive sold-out shows at the Rainbow Theatre, the first time a rock band achieved this.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWooding1978114-55)

### 1974–1980: _Relayer_, _Going for the One_, _Tormato_ and the Paris sessions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1974–1980: Relayer, Going for the One, Tormato and the Paris sessions")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Yes_%28Anderson%2C_Squire%2C_Howe%2C_White%2C_Moraz%29.jpg/250px-Yes_%28Anderson%2C_Squire%2C_Howe%2C_White%2C_Moraz%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_(Anderson,_Squire,_Howe,_White,_Moraz).jpg)

Yes in 1974. Left to right: [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe"), [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"), [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire"), [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)"), and [Patrick Moraz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Moraz "Patrick Moraz")

Several musicians were approached to replace Wakeman, including [Vangelis Papathanassiou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vangelis_Papathanassiou "Vangelis Papathanassiou"), [Eddie Jobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Jobson "Eddie Jobson") of [Roxy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Music "Roxy Music") and former Atlantis/Cat Stevens keyboardist [Jean Roussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Roussel "Jean Roussel"). Howe says he also asked [Keith Emerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Emerson "Keith Emerson"), who did not want to leave [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2021108-56) Yes ultimately chose Swiss keyboardist [Patrick Moraz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Moraz "Patrick Moraz") of [Refugee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_(band) "Refugee (band)"), who arrived in August 1974[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-57) during the recording sessions for _[Relayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relayer "Relayer")_, which took place at Squire's home in [Virginia Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Water "Virginia Water"), Surrey. Released in November that year, _Relayer_ showcased a [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion")-influenced direction the band were pursuing. The album features the 22-minute track titled "[The Gates of Delirium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gates_of_Delirium "The Gates of Delirium")", which highlights a battle initially inspired by _[War and Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_and\_Peace "War and Peace")_ by [Leo Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy "Leo Tolstoy"). Its closing section, "Soon", was subsequently released as a single. The album reached No. 4 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and No. 5 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008154-58) Yes embarked on their [1974–1975 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1960s%E2%80%9370s)#Relayer_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1960s–70s)") to support _Relayer_. The compilation album _[Yesterdays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesterdays\_(Yes\_album) "Yesterdays (Yes album)")_, released in 1975, contained tracks from Yes's first two albums, the B-side track from their "Sweet Dreams" single from 1970 titled "Dear Father", and the original ten-minute version of their cover of "America".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-59)

Between 1975 and 1976, each member of the band released a solo album. Their subsequent [1976 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1960s%E2%80%9370s)#1976_Solo_Albums_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1960s–70s)") of North America with [Peter Frampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Frampton "Peter Frampton") featured some of the band's most-attended shows. The show of 12 June, also supported by [Gary Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Wright "Gary Wright") and [Pousette-Dart Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pousette-Dart_Band "Pousette-Dart Band") at [John F. Kennedy Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_Stadium_(Philadelphia) "John F. Kennedy Stadium (Philadelphia)") in Philadelphia, attracted over 100,000 people.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-60) Roger Dean's brother Martyn was the main designer behind the tour's "Crab Nebula" stage set, while Roger and fabric designer Felicity Youette provided the backgrounds.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Yes_concert.jpg/250px-Yes_concert.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_concert.jpg)

Yes in concert in August 1977. From left to right: [Steve Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Howe "Steve Howe"), [Alan White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_White_(Yes_drummer) "Alan White (Yes drummer)") (behind the drums), [Jon Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Anderson "Jon Anderson"), [Chris Squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Squire "Chris Squire") and [Rick Wakeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Wakeman "Rick Wakeman").

In late 1976, the band travelled to Switzerland and started recording for their album _[Going for the One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Going\_for\_the\_One "Going for the One")_ at [Mountain Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Studios "Mountain Studios"), [Montreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux "Montreux"). It was then that Anderson sent early versions of "Going for the One" and "[Wonderous Stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderous_Stories "Wonderous Stories")" to Wakeman, who felt he could contribute to such material better than the band's past releases. Moraz was let go, after Wakeman was booked initially on a session musician basis, before being convinced by Squire to re-join the band full time.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-61) Upon its release in July 1977, _Going for the One_[topped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_number-one_albums_from_the_1970s_(UK)#1977 "List of number-one albums from the 1970s (UK)") the UK album charts for two weeks[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and reached number 8 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008166-62) "[Wonderous Stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonderous_Stories "Wonderous Stories")" and "Going for the One" were released as singles in the UK and reached numbers 7 and 25, respectively.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008166-62) Although the album's cover was designed by [Hipgnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hipgnosis "Hipgnosis"), it still features their Roger Dean ["bubble" logotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_bubble_logo "Yes bubble logo"). The band's [1977 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1960s%E2%80%9370s)#Going_for_the_One_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1960s–70s)") spanned across six months.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_[Tormato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tormato "Tormato")_ was released in September 1978 at the height of [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") in England, during which the music press criticised Yes as representing the bloated excesses of early-1970s progressive rock. The album saw the band continuing their movement towards shorter songs; no track runs longer than eight minutes.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-63) Wakeman replaced his Mellotrons with the [Birotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birotron "Birotron"), a [tape replay keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampler_(musical_instrument) "Sampler (musical instrument)"), and Squire experimented with harmonisers and [Mu-tron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu-tron "Mu-tron") pedals with his bass. Production was handled collectively by the band and saw disagreements at the mixing stage among the members. With heavy commercial rock-radio airplay, the album reached number 8 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 10 in the US charts, and was also certified platinum (1 million copies sold) by the [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) Despite internal and external criticisms of the album, the band's [1978–1979 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1960s%E2%80%9370s)#Tormato_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1960s–70s)") was a commercial success. Concerts were performed [in the round](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_in_the_round "Theatre in the round") with a £50,000 revolving stage and a 360-degree sound system fitted above it. Their dates at [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden") earned Yes a [Golden Ticket Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden_Gold_Ticket_Award "Madison Square Garden Gold Ticket Award") for grossing over $1 million in box office receipts.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWooding1978197-64)

In October 1979, the band convened in Paris with producer [Roy Thomas Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Thomas_Baker "Roy Thomas Baker"). At the time, Anderson and Wakeman favoured a more fantastical and delicate approach while the rest preferred a heavier rock sound. Howe, Squire and White liked none of the music Anderson was offering at the time as they felt it was too lightweight and lacking in the heaviness that they were generating in their own writing sessions. The Paris sessions abruptly ended in December after White broke his foot while rollerskating in a [roller disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roller_disco "Roller disco").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-lithiummagazine.com_21_March_2014-65)

When the band, minus Wakeman (who had only committed to recording keyboard overdubs once new material would be ready to record), reconvened in February to resume work on the project, their growing musical differences, combined with internal dissension, obstructed progress. Journalist Chris Welch, after attending a rehearsal, noted that Anderson "was singing without his usual conviction and seemed disinclined to talk".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-66) By late March, Howe, Squire and White had begun demoing material as an instrumental trio, increasingly uncertain about Anderson's future involvement. Eventually, a serious band dispute over finance saw Anderson leave Yes, with a dispirited Wakeman departing at around the same time.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1980–1981: _Drama_ and split

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1980–1981: Drama and split")]

In 1980, pop duo [The Buggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Buggles "The Buggles") (singer [Trevor Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Horn "Trevor Horn") and keyboardist [Geoff Downes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Downes "Geoff Downes")) secured the services of [Brian Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Lane_(manager) "Brian Lane (manager)"), who had managed Yes since 1970, as their manager. The Buggles were best known for their 1979 hit single "[Video Killed the Radio Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Killed_the_Radio_Star "Video Killed the Radio Star")" from their album _[The Age of Plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Age\_of\_Plastic "The Age of Plastic")_. At this point, the departure of Anderson and Wakeman had been kept secret from everyone outside the Yes inner circle. Seeing an option of continuing the band with new creative input and expertise, Squire revealed the situation to Horn and Downes and suggested that they join Yes as full-time members. Horn and Downes accepted the invitation and the reconfigured band recorded the _[Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama\_(Yes\_album) "Drama (Yes album)")_ album, which was released in August 1980. The record displayed a heavier, harder sound than the material Yes recorded with Anderson and Wakeman in 1979, opening with the lengthy hard rocker "[Machine Messiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Messiah "Machine Messiah")". The album received substantial radio airplay in the late summer–fall of 1980, and peaked at number 2 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 18 in the US, though it was the first Yes album to not be certified Gold by the RIAA since 1971.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) Their [1980 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#Drama_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)") of North America and the UK received a mixed reaction from audiences. They were well received in the United States and were awarded with a commemorative certificate after they performed a record 16 consecutive sold-out concerts at Madison Square Garden since 1974.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008197-67)

After the _Drama_ tour, Yes reconvened in England to decide the band's next step, beginning by dismissing Lane as their manager. Horn was also dismissed,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-68) and went on to pursue a career in music production, with White and Squire next to depart. Left as the sole remaining members, Downes and Howe opted not to continue with the group and went their own separate ways in December 1980.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_[Yesshows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesshows "Yesshows")_, a live album recorded during 1976 to 1978, mixed in mid-1979 and originally intended for release in late 1979, was released in November 1980, peaking at number 22 in the UK charts[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 43 in the US.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)

An announcement came from the group's management in March 1981 confirming that Yes no longer existed. Downes and Howe soon reunited to form [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_(band) "Asia (band)") with former [King Crimson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Crimson "King Crimson") bassist and vocalist [John Wetton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wetton "John Wetton"), and drummer [Carl Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Palmer "Carl Palmer") from [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"). Squire and White continued to work together, initially recording sessions with [Jimmy Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Page "Jimmy Page") for a proposed band called [XYZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XYZ_(UK_band) "XYZ (UK band)") (short for "ex-Yes-and-Zeppelin") in the spring of 1981. Page's former bandmate [Robert Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plant "Robert Plant") was also to be involved as the vocalist but he lost enthusiasm, citing his ongoing grieving for recently deceased Led Zeppelin drummer [John Bonham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bonham "John Bonham"). The short-lived group produced a few demo tracks, elements of which would appear in Page's band the Firm and on future Yes tracks "Mind Drive" and "Can You Imagine?". In late 1981, Squire and White released "[Run with the Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_with_the_Fox "Run with the Fox")", a Christmas single with Squire on vocals which received radio airplay through the 1980s and early 1990s during the Christmas periods. A second Yes compilation album, _[Classic Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic\_Yes "Classic Yes"),_ was released in November 1981.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-69)

### 1982–1988: First reformation, _90125_ and _Big Generator_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1982–1988: First reformation, 90125 and Big Generator")]

At the beginning of 1982, [Phil Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Carson "Phil Carson") of Atlantic Records introduced Squire and White to guitarist and singer [Trevor Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Rabin "Trevor Rabin"), who had initially made his name with the South African supergroup [Rabbitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbitt "Rabbitt"), subsequently releasing three solo albums, working as a record producer and even briefly considered being a member of [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_(band) "Asia (band)"). The three teamed up in a new band called [Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_(band) "Cinema (band)"), for which Squire also recruited the original Yes keyboard player Tony Kaye. Later in 1982, Cinema entered the studio to record their debut album. Although Rabin and Squire initially shared lead vocals for the project, Trevor Horn was briefly brought into Cinema as a potential singer, but soon opted to become the band's producer instead.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-innerviewsrabin2004-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-71)

Horn worked well with the band. However, his clashes with Tony Kaye (complicated by the fact that Rabin was playing most of the keyboards during the recording sessions) led to Kaye's departure during the recording, though some of his playing was kept on the final album and he had returned by the time it was released.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-innerviewsrabin2004-70) Meanwhile, Squire encountered Jon Anderson (who, since leaving Yes, had released two solo albums and had success with the [Jon and Vangelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_and_Vangelis "Jon and Vangelis") project) at a Los Angeles party and, encouraged by Atlantic Records vice-president [Phil Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Carson "Phil Carson"), played Anderson the Cinema demo tracks. Anderson was then invited into the project as lead singer and joined in April 1983 during the last few weeks of the sessions, having comparatively little creative input beyond adding his lead vocals and re-writing some lyrics.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Rabin_and_Anderson.jpg/250px-Rabin_and_Anderson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rabin_and_Anderson.jpg)

Jon Anderon, Trevor Rabin, and Tony Kaye in 1984

At the suggestion of Carson and other Atlantic executives, Cinema then changed their name to Yes in June 1983. Rabin initially objected to this, as he now found that he had inadvertently joined a reunited band with a history and expectations, rather than help launch a new group.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-72) However, with all the other band members having been members of Yes (with three of them being original members, including the distinctive lead singer) the name change was considered sound commercial strategy.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-78)

Yes released their comeback album _[90125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90125 "90125")_ (named after its catalogue serial number on [Atco Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atco_Records "Atco Records")) in November 1983. The new album marked a significant change in style as the revived Yes had adopted more of a [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") sound with few moments that recalled their progressive rock past. This incarnation of the band has sometimes been informally referred to as "Yes-West", reflecting the band's new base in Los Angeles rather than London.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-80) It became their biggest-selling album, certified by the [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA "RIAA") at triple-platinum (3 million copies) in sales in the US, and introduced the band to younger fans. "Owner of a Lonely Heart" [topped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_number-one_mainstream_rock_hits_(United_States) "List of number-one mainstream rock hits (United States)") the [Hot Mainstream Rock Tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Mainstream_Rock_Tracks "Hot Mainstream Rock Tracks") chart for four weeks and went on to reach the [number-one spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Billboard_Hot_100_number-one_singles_of_1984 "List of Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles of 1984") on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 singles chart, the only single from Yes to do so,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) for two weeks in January 1984. Kaye's short-term replacement on keyboards, [Eddie Jobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Jobson "Eddie Jobson"), appeared briefly in the original video but was edited out as much as possible once Kaye had been persuaded to return to the band.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-81)

In 1984, two further singles from the album "[Leave It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leave_It "Leave It")" and "[It Can Happen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Can_Happen_(Yes_song) "It Can Happen (Yes song)")" reached number 24 and 57 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-82) Yes also earned their only [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") for [Best Rock Instrumental Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rock_Instrumental_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Rock Instrumental Performance") in 1985 for the two-minute track "[Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_(Yes_song) "Cinema (Yes song)")".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-83) They were also nominated for an award for [Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Pop_Performance_by_a_Duo_or_Group_with_Vocals "Grammy Award for Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals") with "Owner of a Lonely Heart", and a [Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rock_Performance_by_a_Duo_or_Group_with_Vocal "Grammy Award for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal") award with _90125_.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-84) The band's [1984–1985 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#9012Live_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)") was the most lucrative in their history and spawned the home video release _[9012Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9012Live\_(video) "9012Live (video)")_, a concert film directed by [Steven Soderbergh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Soderbergh "Steven Soderbergh") with added special effects from [Charlex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlex "Charlex") that cost $1 million.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-85) Issued in 1985, an accompanying live album also appeared that year, _[9012Live: The Solos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9012Live:\_The\_Solos "9012Live: The Solos")_, which earned Yes a nomination for a second Grammy Award for Best Rock Instrumental Performance for Squire's solo track, a rendition of "[Amazing Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing_Grace "Amazing Grace")".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-86)

Yes began recording for their twelfth album, _[Big Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Generator "Big Generator")_, in 1985, initially with Trevor Horn returning as producer. The sessions underwent many starts and stops due to the use of multiple recording locations in Italy, London and Los Angeles, with interpersonal problems leading to Horn leaving the sessions partway through, all of which kept the album from timely completion (the album was intended for a 1986 release, but by the end of that year it was still incomplete).[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-87) Eventually Rabin took over final production. The album was released in September 1987, and immediately began receiving heavy radio airplay, with sales reaching number 17 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 15 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30)_Big Generator_ earned Yes a nomination for a second Grammy Award for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal in 1988, and was also certified platinum (with 1 million-plus in sales) by the RIAA.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-88) The single "[Love Will Find a Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Will_Find_a_Way_(Yes_song) "Love Will Find a Way (Yes song)")" topped the Mainstream Rock chart, while "[Rhythm of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_of_Love_(Yes_song) "Rhythm of Love (Yes song)")" reached number 2 and "[Shoot High Aim Low](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_High_Aim_Low "Shoot High Aim Low")" number 11.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) The [1987–1988 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#Big_Generator_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)") ended with an appearance at Madison Square Garden on 14 May 1988 as part of [Atlantic Records 40th anniversary concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records_40th_Anniversary "Atlantic Records 40th Anniversary").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1988–1995: _Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe_, _Union_ and _Talk_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1988–1995: Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe, Union and Talk")]

By the end of 1988, Anderson felt creatively sidelined by Rabin and Squire and had grown tired of the musical direction of the "Yes-West" line-up. He took leave of the band, asserting that he would never stay in Yes purely for the money, and started work in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") and [Montserrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montserrat "Montserrat") on an ostensible solo project that eventually involved Wakeman, Howe and Bruford. This collaboration led to suggestions that there would be some kind of reformation of the "classic" Yes, although the Monserrat sessions brought in bass player [Tony Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Levin "Tony Levin"), whom Bruford had worked with in King Crimson. The project, rather than taking over or otherwise using the Yes name, was called [Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anderson_Bruford_Wakeman_Howe "Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe") (ABWH).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Their [eponymous album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anderson_Bruford_Wakeman_Howe_(album) "Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe (album)"), released in June 1989, featured "Brother of Mine", which became an MTV hit and went gold in the United States. It later emerged that the four band members had not all recorded together; Anderson and producer [Chris Kimsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Kimsey "Chris Kimsey") slotted their parts into place. Howe has stated publicly that he was unhappy with the mix of his guitars on the album,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-Innerviews-89) though a version of "Fist of Fire" with more of Howe's guitars left intact appeared on the _[In a Word: Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_a\_Word:\_Yes\_(1969-) "In a Word: Yes (1969-)")_ box set in 2002. ABWH toured in [1989 and 1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#Anderson_Bruford_Wakeman_Howe_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)") as "An Evening of Yes Music" which featured Levin, keyboardist [Julian Colbeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Colbeck "Julian Colbeck"), and guitarist [Milton McDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_McDonald "Milton McDonald") as support musicians. A live album and home video were recorded and released in 1993, both titled _[An Evening of Yes Music Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Evening\_of\_Yes\_Music\_Plus "An Evening of Yes Music Plus")_ that featured [Jeff Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Berlin "Jeff Berlin") on bass due to Levin suffering from illness. The tour was also dogged by legal battles sparked by Atlantic Records due to the band's references to Yes in promotional materials and the tour title.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Following the tour, the group returned to the recording studio to produce their second album, tentatively called _Dialogue_. After hearing the tracks, [Arista Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arista_Records "Arista Records") refused to release the album as they felt the initial mixes and material were weak.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-90) They encouraged the group to seek outside songwriters, preferably ones who could help them deliver hit singles. Meanwhile, the "Yes-West" group had been working on a follow-up to _Big Generator_ and had been shopping around for a new singer, auditioning [Roger Hodgson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Hodgson "Roger Hodgson") of [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp"), [Steve Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Walsh_(musician) "Steve Walsh (musician)") of [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_(band) "Kansas (band)"), [Billy Sherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Sherwood "Billy Sherwood") of [World Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_(band) "World Trade (band)") and solo pop/dance singer [Robbie Nevil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbie_Nevil "Robbie Nevil") (who'd scored a US #2 hit in 1986 with "[C'est la Vie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C'est_la_Vie_(Robbie_Nevil_song) "C'est la Vie (Robbie Nevil song)")").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-91) Walsh only spent one day with the band, but Sherwood and Squire quickly established a rapport and continued with writing sessions, although Sherwood ultimately chose not to formally join the group or become the lead singer.

At this point, rather than approaching outside songwriters as suggested by Arista, Anderson approached Rabin. Rabin sent Anderson a demo tape with three songs, indicating that ABWH could have one but had to send the others back. Arista listened to them and wanted all of them. Arista now suggested that the "Yes-West" group, with Anderson on vocals, record the songs from Rabin's demo tape and add them to the incomplete ABWH album: this then led to the suggestion of creating a combined album with both Yes factions,[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-92) which would then be released as a full album under the Yes name.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]_[Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union\_(Yes\_album) "Union (Yes album)")_ was released in April 1991 and is the thirteenth studio album from Yes. The album does not feature all eight members playing at once: instead, each group played their own songs, with only Anderson singing on all tracks. Squire sang background vocals on a few of the ABWH tracks, with Tony Levin playing all the bass on those songs. The track "Masquerade" earned Yes a Grammy Award nomination for Best Rock Instrumental Performance in 1992:[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-93)

Almost the entire band have openly stated their dislike of _Union_.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008324%E2%80%93325-94) Bruford has disowned the album entirely, and Wakeman was reportedly unable to recognise any of his keyboard work in the final edit and threw his copy of the album out of his limousine.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008420-95) He has since referred to the album as "Onion" because it makes him cry when he thinks about it. _Union_ co-producer [Jonathan Elias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Elias "Jonathan Elias") later stated publicly in an interview that Anderson, as the associate producer, knew of the session musicians' involvement. He added that he and Anderson had even initiated their contributions, because hostility between some of the ABWH band members at the time was preventing work from being accomplished.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-96) Howe would describe the Grammy nomination for "Masquerade" (a track he had recorded solo at home) as "pure justice", following the difficulties he'd had with making the album.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorse199691-97)

_Union_ sold approximately 1.5 million copies worldwide, and peaked at number 7 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 15 in the US charts.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) Two singles from the album were released. "[Lift Me Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lift_Me_Up_(Yes_song) "Lift Me Up (Yes song)")" topped the Mainstream Rock charts in May 1991 for six weeks, while "[Saving My Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saving_My_Heart "Saving My Heart")" peaked at number 9.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) The [1991–1992 Union tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#Union_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)") united all eight members on a revolving circular stage.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-98) In August 1991, while the _Union_ tour was underway, Atlantic released _[Yesyears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesyears "Yesyears")_, a four-CD box set anthology. Two accompanying home videos, _[Yesyears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesyears\_(video) "Yesyears (video)")_ and _[Greatest Video Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest\_Video\_Hits\_(Yes\_video) "Greatest Video Hits (Yes video)")_, were also released during 1991.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Following the tour's conclusion in 1992, Bruford chose not to remain involved with Yes and returned to his jazz project _[Earthworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthworks\_(album) "Earthworks (album)")_. In 1993, the album _[Symphonic Music of Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic\_Music\_of\_Yes "Symphonic Music of Yes")_ was released, featuring orchestrated Yes tracks arranged by [Dee Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Palmer "Dee Palmer"). Howe, Bruford and Anderson perform on the record, joined by the [London Philharmonic Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Philharmonic_Orchestra "London Philharmonic Orchestra"), the [English Chamber Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Chamber_Orchestra "English Chamber Orchestra") and the [London Community Gospel Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Community_Gospel_Choir "London Community Gospel Choir"). Howe and Bruford performed together on television (presented as "Yes") to promote the album, marking Bruford's final performance under the Yes name before retiring from performing.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-99)

The next Yes studio album, as with _Union_, was masterminded by a record company rather than by the band itself.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch2008336-100) Victory Music had approached Rabin with a proposal to produce an album solely with the _90125_ line-up. Rabin initially countered by requesting that Wakeman also be included: Bruford had already departed from the band again, while Howe was not invited to be involved with the new project. Rabin began assembling the album at his home, using the then-pioneering concept of a digital home studio, and used material written by himself and Anderson.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-101) By 1993 the new album was well into production, but Wakeman's involvement had finally been cancelled, as his refusal to leave his long-serving management created insuperable legal problems.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

_[Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk\_(Yes\_album) "Talk (Yes album)")_ was released in March 1994 and is the band's fourteenth studio release. Its cover was designed by [pop artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_art "Pop art")[Peter Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Max "Peter Max"). The record was largely composed and performed by Rabin, with the other band members following Rabin's tracks for their respective instrumentation.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-ultimateclassicrock-102) It was digitally recorded and produced by Rabin with engineer Michael Jay, using 3.4 [GB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigabyte "Gigabyte") of hard disk storage split among four networked [Apple Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Macintosh "Apple Macintosh") computers running [Digital Performer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Performer "Digital Performer"). The album blended elements of radio-friendly rock with a more structurally ambitious approach taken from the band's progressive blueprint, with the fifteen-minute track "[Endless Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless_Dream_(Yes_song) "Endless Dream (Yes song)")". The album reached number 20 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 33 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) The track "[The Calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Calling_(Yes_song) "The Calling (Yes song)")" reached number 2 on the _Billboard_[Hot Mainstream Rock Tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Mainstream_Rock_Tracks "Hot Mainstream Rock Tracks") chart and "[Walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walls_(Yes_song) "Walls (Yes song)")", which Rabin had written with former [Supertramp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertramp "Supertramp") songwriter and co-founder [Roger Hodgson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Hodgson "Roger Hodgson"), peaked at number 24.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40) It also became Yes's second-last-charting single.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-SomethingElse-103) Rabin and Hodgson wrote a lot of material together and became close friends.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-SomethingElse-103) Yes performed "Walls" on Late Show with David Letterman on 20 June 1994.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-morningcall1994-104) The [1994 tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#Talk_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)") (for which the band employed Billy Sherwood as a support musician on additional guitar, bass, vocals and keyboards) used a sound system developed by Rabin named Concertsonics which allowed the audience located in certain seating areas to tune portable FM radios to a specific frequency, so they could hear the concert with headphones.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-105)

In early 1995, following the tour, disagreements and dissatisfactions forced another change in the band. 1990s Yes manager Jon Brewer has stated that Squire had not appreciated the _Talk_ production process - "(He) didn't like that. He didn't think it was what Yes was all about; he was very much against a computerised, digital sound at that time. So Trevor and Chris moved away from one another for quite a while."[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-106) For his part, Rabin felt that he had achieved his highest ambitions with _Talk_ and lamented its disappointing reception, feeling that this was due to the fact that it "just wasn't what people wanted to hear at the time." Having remarked at the conclusion of the tour "I think I'm done", Rabin quit the band and returned to Los Angeles, where he shifted his focus to composing for films.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-ultimateclassicrock-102) Kaye also left Yes to pursue other projects.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1995–2000: _Keys to Ascension_, _Open Your Eyes_ and _The Ladder_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1995–2000: Keys to Ascension, Open Your Eyes and The Ladder")]

In November 1995, Anderson, Squire and White resurrected the "classic" 1970s line-up of Yes by inviting Wakeman and Howe back to the band, recording two new lengthy tracks called "Be the One" and "That, That Is". In March 1996 Yes performed three live shows at the [Fremont Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fremont_Theater "Fremont Theater") in [San Luis Obispo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Luis_Obispo "San Luis Obispo"), California which were recorded and released, along with the new studio tracks, that October on [CMC International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMC_International "CMC International") Records as the _[Keys to Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keys\_to\_Ascension "Keys to Ascension")_ album, which peaked at number 48 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 99 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) A same-titled [live video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keys_to_Ascension_(video) "Keys to Ascension (video)") of the shows was also released that year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Yes continued to record new tracks in the studio, drawing some material written around the time of the XYZ project. At one point the new songs were to be released as a studio album, but commercial considerations meant that the new tracks were eventually packaged with the remainder of the 1996 San Luis Obispo shows in November 1997 on _[Keys to Ascension 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keys\_to\_Ascension\_2 "Keys to Ascension 2")_. The record managed to reach number 62 in the UK,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) but failed to chart in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) Disgruntled at the way a potential studio album had been sacrificed in favour of the _Keys to Ascension_ releases (as well as the way in which a Yes tour was being arranged without his input or agreement), Wakeman left the group again. (The studio material from both albums would eventually be compiled and re-released without the live tracks onto a single CD, 2001's _[Keystudio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystudio "Keystudio")_.)[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

With Yes in disarray again, Squire turned to Billy Sherwood (by now the band's engineer) for help.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-se-sherwood102013-107) Both men had been working on a side project called [Conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conspiracy_(band) "Conspiracy (band)") and reworked two existing demo recordings from there to turn them into Yes songs. Encouraged by this, they then created new material with Anderson and White (Howe's involvement at this stage was minimal, mainly taking place towards the end of the sessions). Sherwood's integral involvement with the writing, production, and performance of the music led to his finally joining Yes as a full member (taking on the role of harmony singer, keyboardist and second guitarist).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The results of the sessions were released in November 1997 as the seventeenth Yes studio album, _[Open Your Eyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open\_Your\_Eyes\_(Yes\_album) "Open Your Eyes (Yes album)")_ (on the Beyond Music label, who ensured that the group had greater control in packaging and naming). The music (mainly at Sherwood's urging) attempted to bridge the differing Yes styles of the 1970s and 1980s.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-se-sherwood102013-107) (Sherwood: "My goal was to try to break down those partisan walls…For that, I am proud—to have aligned planets for a moment in time."[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-se-sherwood102013-107)) However, _Open Your Eyes_ was not a chart success; the record peaked at number 151 on the _Billboard_ 200[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) but failed to enter the charts in the UK. The [title single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Your_Eyes_(Yes_song) "Open Your Eyes (Yes song)") managed to reach number 33 on the mainstream rock chart.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicsinglechart-40)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Yes_19980619.jpg/250px-Yes_19980619.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_19980619.jpg)

Yes in 1998

For the [1997/1998 _Open Your Eyes_ tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#Open_Your_Eyes_and_Thirtieth_Anniversary_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)"), Yes hired Russian keyboard player [Igor Khoroshev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_Khoroshev "Igor Khoroshev"), who had played on some of the album tracks. Significantly, the tour setlist featured only a few pieces from the new album, and mostly concentrated on earlier material. Anderson and Howe, who had been less involved with the writing and production on _Open Your Eyes_ than they'd wished, would express dissatisfaction about the album later.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

By the time the band came to record their eighteenth studio album _[The Ladder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ladder\_(Yes\_album) "The Ladder (Yes album)")_ with producer [Bruce Fairbairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Fairbairn "Bruce Fairbairn"), Khoroshev had become a full-time member (with Sherwood now concentrating on songwriting, vocal arrangements and second guitar). With Khoroshev's classically influenced keyboard style, and with all members now making more or less equal writing contributions, the band's sound found a balance between its eclectic 1970s progressive rock style and the more polished pop sound sought on the previous album. _The Ladder_ also featured Latin music ingredients and clear world music influences, mostly brought in by Alan White (although Fairbairn's multi-instrumentalist colleague [Randy Raine-Reusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Raine-Reusch "Randy Raine-Reusch") made a strong contribution to the album's textures). One of the album tracks, "Homeworld (The Ladder)", was written for Relic Entertainment's [Homeworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeworld "Homeworld"), a real-time strategy computer game, and was used as the credits and outro theme. Pleased with the result of the album's creation, the band had been in tentative discussions to continue work with Fairbairn on future projects, but he died suddenly during the final mixing sessions of the album.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-108)

_The Ladder_ was released in September 1999, peaking at number 36 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 99 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) While [on tour in 1999 and early 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(1980s%E2%80%9390s)#The_Ladder_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (1980s–90s)"), Yes recorded their performance at the [House of Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blues "House of Blues") in [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas_Valley "Las Vegas Valley") on 31 October 1999, releasing it in September 2000 as a live album and DVD called _[House of Yes: Live from House of Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_of\_Yes:\_Live\_from\_House\_of\_Blues "House of Yes: Live from House of Blues")_. As Sherwood saw his role in Yes as creating and performing new music, while the rest of the band now wished to concentrate on performing the back catalogue, he amicably resigned from Yes at the end of the tour.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-se-sherwood102013-107)

In summer 2000, Yes embarked on the three-month [Masterworks tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(2000s%E2%80%9310s)#Masterworks_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (2000s–10s)") of the United States, on which they performed only material which had been released between 1970 and 1974 (_The Yes Album_ through to _Relayer_). While on tour, Khoroshev was involved in a backstage incident of sexual assault with a female security guard at Nissan Pavilion in [Bristow, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristow,_Virginia "Bristow, Virginia") on 23 July 2000[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-111) and parted company with the band at the end of the tour.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 2001–2008: _Magnification_, Anniversary touring, and Anderson's departure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yes_(band)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2001–2008: Magnification, Anniversary touring, and Anderson's departure")]

Following the departures of Sherwood and Khoroshev and the death of Fairbairn, Yes once again set about reinventing themselves, this time choosing to record without a keyboardist, opting instead to include a 60-piece orchestra conducted by [Larry Groupé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Group%C3%A9 "Larry Groupé"); the first time the band used an orchestra since _Time and a Word_ in 1970. The result was their nineteenth studio album, 2001's _[Magnification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnification\_(album) "Magnification (album)")_. The record was not a chart success; it peaked at number 71 in the UK[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) and number 186 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) The Yes Symphonic Tour ran from July to December 2001 and had the band performing on stage with an orchestra and American keyboardist [Tom Brislin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Brislin "Tom Brislin"). Their two shows in Amsterdam, in November, were recorded for their 2002 DVD and 2009 CD release _[Symphonic Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic\_Live "Symphonic Live")_. The band invited Wakeman to play with them for the filming, but he was on a solo tour at the time.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-112)

Following Wakeman's announcement of his return in April 2002, Yes embarked on their [Full Circle Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(2000s%E2%80%9310s)#Full_Circle_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (2000s–10s)") in 2002–2003 that included their first performances in Australia since 1973.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-billboard03-113) The band's appearance in [Montreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux "Montreux") on this tour was documented on the album and DVD _[Live at Montreux 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_at\_Montreux\_2003 "Live at Montreux 2003")_, released in 2007. In 2002, [Rhino Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhino_Records "Rhino Records") issued _[In a Word: Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_a\_Word:\_Yes\_(1969%E2%80%93) "In a Word: Yes (1969–)")_, a five CD box set of classic, rare and unreleased tracks from the band's history, including some from the 1979 Paris sessions, followed a year later by the compilation album _[The Ultimate Yes: 35th Anniversary Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ultimate\_Yes:\_35th\_Anniversary\_Collection "The Ultimate Yes: 35th Anniversary Collection")_, which reached number 10 in the UK charts,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-officialchartsuk-26) their highest-charting album since 1991, and number 131 in the US[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-allmusicalbumchart-30) During 2003 and 2004, Rhino also released remastered editions of all Yes' studio albums up to, and including, _90125_, all featuring rare and previously unreleased bonus tracks. These editions would be collected in 2013 as _[The Studio Albums 1969–1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Studio\_Albums\_1969%E2%80%931987 "The Studio Albums 1969–1987")_ box set, with _Big Generator_ also receiving the same treatment.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] On 18 March 2003, minor planet [(7707) Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7707_Yes "7707 Yes") was named in honour of the band.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-114)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Yes_at_Air_Canada_Centre%2C_May_7th%2C_2004_%28292858662%29.jpg/250px-Yes_at_Air_Canada_Centre%2C_May_7th%2C_2004_%28292858662%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yes_at_Air_Canada_Centre,_May_7th,_2004_(292858662).jpg)

Yes in 2004

On 26 January 2004, the film _[Yesspeak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yesspeak "Yesspeak")_ premiered in a number of select theatres, followed by a closed-circuit live acoustic performance of the group. Both _Yesspeak_ and the acoustic performance, titled _[Yes Acoustic: Guaranteed No Hiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes\_Acoustic:\_Guaranteed\_No\_Hiss "Yes Acoustic: Guaranteed No Hiss")_, were released on DVD later that year. A [35th anniversary tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Yes_concert_tours_(2000s%E2%80%9310s)#35th_Anniversary_Tour "List of Yes concert tours (2000s–10s)") followed in 2004 which was documented on the DVD _[Songs from Tsongas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs\_from\_Tsongas "Songs from Tsongas")_, released in 2005.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-115) After their 35th Anniversary Tour, Yes described themselves as "on hiatus".[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe2021227%E2%80%9328,_234-116)

During the hiatus, Yes members continued to collaborate. Chicago band The Mob were an eight-piece ensemble, they formed in 1966 & were the first group from Chicago to include a full horn section (the Chicago Horn Rock Sound). They played alongside & often backed other acts such as Lou Christie, the Young Rascals & Sam the Sham, their music was deemed as mod music & was aimed at young people with a liking for soul music. They broke up in 1975 but in 2011 they were inducted into the South Dakota Rock & Roll Music Association at the Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls, SD, more than 2,000 people in attendance saw and heard The MOB in person, their first reunion in 35 years.

They recorded this great track, popular on the Carolinas Beach Music & Northern Soul scenes in 1970, on the US Colossus & UK Polydor labels, "I Dig Everything About You".

Chicago band The Mob were an eight-piece ensemble, they formed in 1966 & were the first group from Chicago to include a full horn section (the Chicago Horn Rock Sound). They played alongside & often backed other acts such as Lou Christie, the Young Rascals & Sam the Sham, their music was deemed as mod music & was aimed at young people with a liking for soul music. They broke up in 1975 but in 2011 they were inducted into the South Dakota Rock & Roll Music Association at the Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls, SD, more than 2,000 people in attendance saw and heard The MOB in person, their first reunion in 35 years.

They recorded this great track, popular on the Carolinas Beach Music & Northern Soul scenes in 1970, on the US Colossus & UK Polydor labels, "I Dig Everything About You".

# History of the Band

The WVU Marching Band was formed 125 years ago in 1901 as an all-male ROTC band of eight members with Walter Mestrezat serving as the band’s first director.

![Image 3: Walter Mestrezat](https://bands.wvu.edu/files/f43b942d-2897-42d4-9ac5-5cee615f96dc/200x286?cb=715cffb9594b41520c84129c050dad19)

Walter Mestrezat

 Since every male attending the University at that time was required to take Military Science (ROTC), the Military Band provided the appropriate music for the military revues and parades. They also marched at football halftimes, at major community celebrations and parades, and for important campus events, always in strict military style. 

  

In 1925, a group of eleven non-ROTC males were allowed to join the band, but were not permitted the same monetary benefits as those enrolled military band members. Feeling that this was an unfair practice, the eleven decided to form their own marching band. This "rebel" band of musicians wanted to also perform at halftime and did in fact receive permission from Director Mestrezat and the athletic director. However, when then WVU President Frank Trotter heard about the possibility of two bands, he moved quickly to rectify this situation. The "rebel" group had to first become a legitimate student organization to even be recognized. This group quickly pledged a Greek fraternity and formed what is now WVU’s Omicron chapter of Kappa Kappa Psi. It wasn’t until years later that the two bands merged into one true University Marching Band.

  

 After serving for 37 years as its director and increasing the band's size to approximately 70 members, Mestrezat stepped down as director and Bernard McGregor assumed the position in 1938. McGregor served a 13-year span as the band's director, but was on leave for one year due to his military duty in World War II. During that year, Clifford Brown, who later became assistant dean of the College of Creative Arts, served as the band's director on an interim basis.

  

![Image 4: marching band on the field in the 1960s](https://bands.wvu.edu/files/6a4a5b1e-954b-4bd1-8a75-b270e5839e57/999x802?cb=7ddc3844d4a1e02719b8bd7f91313eb2)

Marching band practicing, c. 1966

 The modern era for the Mountaineer Marching Band began in the 1950's and 1960's with Larry Intravaia and Budd Udell serving as the directors. Two other gentlemen, Richard Strange and Frank Borkowski, also served as marching band directors during this time - each serving for one year. Outstanding arrangements and creativity began to bring recognition to the group. Both of the University's fight songs, "Fight Mountaineers" and "Hail West Virginia" were arranged for the band by Budd Udell and are, in fact, the same arrangements the band plays today. In 1970, Gerald Zimmerman served a one-year appointment as the band's director.

  

 In 1971, Don Wilcox came to WVU as Director of Bands. During the 1970's, the WVU Marching Band experienced rapid growth and impressive development, during which it more than tripled in size, gained a national reputation, and saw major changes in attitude, desire, and dedication. For his first year, Wilcox inherited an all-male band of 88 members. This membership changed in 1972 when Wilcox encouraged women to join the program for the first time. During the early '70's, the band performed at several prestigious events such as area NFL games and two Peach Bowls in Atlanta. The phrase "The Pride of West Virginia" was first used by the 1975 Peach Bowl announcer; eventually it became the band's official nickname.

  

![Image 5: marching band in the 1970s on football field](https://bands.wvu.edu/files/25251fb9-a200-4727-b2f3-df053528b2b9/624x632?cb=7ed6a33b4ba6ae6370651b02c622346e)

The band on the field in 1977

The middle and late 1970's saw a new set of uniforms and a steady increase in membership. Because of the unsurpassed pride and desire for high performance standards, the band grew to 280 members by the end of the decade. Several "highs" were achieved during this time with trips to Kentucky, Penn State, Virginia Tech, Oklahoma, and New York City. The '79 Band set the highest standards yet, and ended the season with a very special "Goodbye to Mountaineer Field" show as Old Mountaineer Field saw its last football game.

  

 The 1980's opened with a new stadium, a new football coach (Don Nehlen), and a marching band of over 300 members. Throughout the '80's and the '90's, the band achieved many new levels. Not only did the band introduce two new sets of uniforms to the delight of Mountaineer fans during this time, but it also served as host to several events including summer shows by Drum Corps International and many annual Eastern Regional Competitions of Bands of America. Because of the continued success of the football team, the band also had the opportunity to travel to many exciting bowl games throughout the country, including the Peach Bowl, Hall of Fame Bowl, Bluebonnet Bowl, Sun Bowl, Fiesta Bowl, Sugar Bowl, Carquest Bowl, and Gator Bowl!

  

 During these decades, the band traveled to almost every county in West Virginia. This increased statewide exposure, along with its participation in the University sponsored "WVU Days" program, the annual "KeyNotes" concerts, and its continuing off-campus performances, led to the WVU Band's growing recognition during the 1990's as an ambassador throughout the state of West Virginia. The band also traveled during these years to several regular season games at sites that included Virginia Tech, Pittsburgh, Maryland, Syracuse, and Purdue. In 1995, the band expanded its recordings to include their first compact disc.

  

![Image 6: Sudler award presentation](https://bands.wvu.edu/files/43b678ca-60b6-4621-9fde-41c2293836de/225x211?cb=d6c03c51be9ef192454b7e1abcbb0748)

Sudler Trophy presentation

Arguably the most important event in the first century of the WVU Marching Band’s history took place in 1997 when the band was selected as the recipient of the John Philip Sousa Foundation's "Sudler Trophy." This prestigious award honored the WVU Marching Band as the nation's outstanding collegiate marching band for that year. The Sudler Trophy recognized the long-standing tradition of dedication, commitment, and pride by the band’s present and past members, staff, and directors. The trophy was awarded by the officers of the John Philip Sousa Foundation at the 1997 Homecoming game with over 500 members of the Alumni Band joining the 330-member WVU Marching Band for the special presentation. Today, the Sudler Trophy is proudly displayed in the office of the WVU Bands in the Creative Arts Center.

  

 At the end of the 1997 "Sudler Season," and after 27 years as the marching band director, Don Wilcox promoted Assistant Director John Hendricks, making him the 10th director of the WVU Marching Band. Under John Hendricks' leadership, the 1998 WVU Marching Band continued achieving milestones by being the largest band in the University's history at that time with over 380 members! New standards of performance excellence were achieved by the bands of the late 1990's and early 2000's.The band traveled to several away games including those in Charlotte (NC), Cincinnati (OH), College Park (MD), Blacksburg (VA), and Notre Dame (IN). During this time, the group also traveled to the Insight.com Bowl, the Music City Bowl, the Continental Tire Bowl, and twice to the Gator Bowl.

  

 Besides the start of a new era of WVU football with Coach Rich Rodriguez, the 2001 season was very special for the WVU Band with the celebration of its 100th anniversary. The culmination of the centennial festivities occurred at Homecoming, when the band was joined by over 500 members of the Alumni Band for a rousing pregame tunnel entrance, which soon spread to cover the entire field! The 850-member mass band closed this special anniversary halftime show with one of the most popular halftime selections in the WVU Band's library - "Walk Him Up the Stairs/Old Man River."

  

[![Image 7: saxophone player in 1983](https://bands.wvu.edu/files/a3fde2ff-26d7-40a1-bc6e-c5cb13c8b6cb/800x823?cb=0fdb98f3a876b5276459e37c58e566ae)](https://wvubands.sandbox.wvu.edu/files/d/a3fde2ff-26d7-40a1-bc6e-c5cb13c8b6cb/1983-band.jpg)

The band performing in 1983

At the end of the 2004-2005 academic year, Don Wilcox retired after a prestigious 34-year career at WVU. John Hendricks replaced Wilcox as WVU's Director of Bands and Assistant Director Jay Drury was named the 11th director of the WVU Marching Band. During the 2005 season, the WVU Band performed on the grounds of the US Capitol as part of the national "Constitution Day" festivities, as well as at WVU's first BCS Bowl Game, the Nokia Sugar Bowl, in Atlanta, Georgia. The 2006 season featured a brand-new set of uniforms, a record-breaking "Band Aid" fundraising campaign by the WVU Foundation, and a Gator Bowl victory with a second consecutive top-ten finish for the WVU Football team. 2007 was also a successful season for the band as the WVU Foundation instituted the "Pride Travel Fund" to help defer the cost of band travel. The group performed in several locations around the country, including at the 2008 Tostitos Fiesta Bowl in Glendale, AZ where the Mountaineers defeated Oklahoma under then interim head coach Bill Stewart and finished in the top-ten for a third consecutive season!

  

 The 2008 season had the distinction of seeing the largest WVU Marching Band ever, as the band topped 390 members as band camp began. A great trip to New York City and the UConn game highlighted the regular season, as well as a 4th consecutive bowl victory for the Mountaineers and sharing the final game with WVU quarterback Pat White. The 2009 season featured another outstanding 370+ member band and featured a trip to SEC country to play the Auburn Tigers in Alabama and concluded with an 8th consecutive bowl appearance as the band performed in Florida at Universal Studios in Orlando and in Jacksonville as part of the 2010 Gator Bowl. The 2009 season also marked the end of an era for the band's old "crow's nest" as a new "state-of-the-art" rehearsal tower has been constructed at the band practice site. In 2010, the band once again traveled extensively, with the highlight being a trip to the LSU game in Baton Rouge, Louisiana and a visit to New Orleans; the longest regular-season trip in WVU Band history at that time. A visit to Orlando, FL for the Champs Sports Bowl, including another performance at Universal Studios, was the band's 9th consecutive bowl trip and topped off another successful season for "The Pride."

  

![Image 8: band forming the letters WVU on the football field](https://bands.wvu.edu/files/f6aa6e34-cba2-4668-bad3-dc6ef00a9e67/877x715?cb=08f86f8686336e975f53caf87ec86225)

The band in formation in 1967

The 2011 season marked the first season of WVU Football under new Head Coach Dana Holgorsen and the final season for WVU as a member of the Big East Conference. Highlights for the band included final conference game trips to Cincinnati and Rutgers, which included a visit to New York City. With the success of the 2011 WVU Football Team, the band ended the season with an exciting trip to Miami, FL for WVU's 10th consecutive bowl game and 3rd BCS Bowl victory as the Mountaineers defeated the Clemson Tigers in the 2012 Discover Orange Bowl! 2012 marked the inaugural season for WVU in the Big XII Conference, and featured home games with Oklahoma, Baylor, TCU, Kansas, and Kansas State at Mountaineer Field. The band traveled to Washington, D.C. to perform at FedEx Field, the home of the NFL's Washington Redskins, for the WVU vs. James Madison Game. The season concluded with a trip to the band's 11th consecutive bowl game at the Pinstripe Bowl in New York City at Yankee Stadium. The 2013 Season featured the band's first trip to a Big XII conference school for the game against Oklahoma and a big home victory over No. 11 ranked Oklahoma State! 2014 featured a trip to Atlanta for the kickoff game vs. Alabama and to Maryland for the Mountaineers' big win over the Terrapins. Both trips featured combined band performances as "The Pride" shared the field with The Alabama "Million Dollar Band" and the "Mighty Sound of Maryland." The band also enjoyed a fun trip to the AutoZone Liberty Bowl in Memphis, TN to close out the season.

  

 In 2015 the band experienced a performance at the Pittsburgh Steelers vs. San Francisco 49ers NFL game at Heinz Field in Pittsburgh, WVU's first home victory over traditional conference powerhouse Texas, sharing the field with Country Music Superstar Brad Paisley for a nationally televised ABC TV special, and the unveiling of a brand new set of Uniforms! The band also enjoyed a fun trip to Phoenix, Arizona for the big bowl win over Arizona State in the Cactus Bowl at Chase Field - the home of Major League Baseball's Arizona Diamondbacks!

  

Highlighting the start of the WVU Marching Band’s second century of existence was the band’s appearances in the 2024 and 2016 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. "The Pride of West Virginia” marched through the streets of New York City performing the WVU fight song, "Hail West Virginia!" along with one of the band’s signature tunes, “Country Roads."

  

 Throughout its 125-year history, the Mountaineer Marching Band has grown and evolved into an active, high-spirited organization with great tradition. To the citizens of the state of West Virginia (and beyond), the Pride exemplifies WVU. The esprit de corps of the group, its tradition of excellence in performance, and the enthusiastic audience response to the sights and sounds of the band have brought great recognition to the both the band and the university throughout the country. The members take great pride in not only maintaining this rich legacy, but building on it as they strive to reach new heights.
